text: Bhagavad Gita 1.1 — Dhritarashtra said: What did my (people) and the Pandavas do, O Sanjaya! when they assembled together on the holy field of Kurukshetra, desirous to do battle?
Bhagavad Gita 1.2 — Sanjaya said: Seeing the army of the Pandavas drawn up in battle-array, the prince Duryodhana approached the preceptor, and spoke (these) words.
Bhagavad Gita 1.3 — O preceptor! observe this grand army of the sons of Pandu, drawn up in battle-array by your talented pupil, the son of Drupada.
Bhagavad Gita 1.4 — In it are heroes (bearing) large bows, the equals of Bhima and Arjuna in battle—(namely), Yuyudhana, Virata, and Drupada, the master of a great car.
Bhagavad Gita 1.5 — And Dhrishtaketu, Chekitana, and the valiant king of Kasi, Purujit and Kuntibhoja, and that eminent man Saibya.
Bhagavad Gita 1.6 — The heroic Yudhamanyu, the valiant Uttamaujas, the son of Subhadra, and the sons of Draupadi—all masters of great cars.
Bhagavad Gita 1.7 — And now, O best of Brahmanas! learn who are most distinguished among us, and are leaders of my army. I will name them to you, in order that you may know them well.
Bhagavad Gita 1.8 — Yourself, and Bhishma, and Karna, and Kripa the victor of (many) battles; Asvatthaman, and Vikarna, and also the son of Somadatta.
Bhagavad Gita 1.9 — And many other brave men, who have given up their lives for me, who fight with various weapons, (and are) all dextrous in battle.
Bhagavad Gita 1.10 — Thus our army which is protected by Bhishma is unlimited; while this army of theirs which is protected by Bhima is very limited.
Bhagavad Gita 1.11 — And therefore do ye all, occupying respectively the positions assigned to you, protect Bhishma only.
Bhagavad Gita 1.12 — Then his powerful grandsire, Bhishma, the oldest of the Kauravas, roaring aloud like a lion, blew his conch, (thereby) affording delight to Duryodhana.
Bhagavad Gita 1.13 — And then all at once, conchs, and kettledrums, and tabors, and trumpets were played upon; and there was a tumultuous din.
Bhagavad Gita 1.14 — Then, too, Madhava and the son of Pandu (Arjuna), seated in a grand chariot to which white steeds were yoked, blew their heavenly conchs.
Bhagavad Gita 1.15 — Hrishikesa blew the Panchajanya, and Dhananjaya the Devadatta, and Bhima, (the doer) of fearful deeds, blew the great conch Paundra.
Bhagavad Gita 1.16 — King Yudhishthira, the son of Kunti, blew the Anantavijaya, and Nakula and Sahadeva (respectively) the Sughosha and Manipushpaka.
Bhagavad Gita 1.17 — And the king of Kasi, too, who has an excellent bow, and Sikhandin, the master of a great car, and Dhrishtadyumna, Virata, and the unconquered Satyaki.
Bhagavad Gita 1.18 — And Drupada, and the sons of Draupadi, and the son of Subhadra, of mighty arms, blew conchs severally from all sides, O king of the earth!
Bhagavad Gita 1.19 — That tumultuous din rent the hearts of all (the people) of Dhritarashtra's (party), causing reverberations throughout heaven and earth.

Bhagavad Gita 1.20 — Then seeing (the people of) Dhritarashtra's party regularly marshalled, the son of Pandu, whose standard is the ape, raised his bow, after the discharge of missiles had commenced.
Bhagavad Gita 1.21 — And O king of the earth! spake these words to Hrishikesa: O undegraded one! station my chariot between the two armies.
Bhagavad Gita 1.22 — While I observe those, who stand here desirous to engage in battle, and with whom, in the labours of this struggle, I must do battle.
Bhagavad Gita 1.23 — I will observe those who are assembled here and who are about to engage in battle, wishing to do service in battle to the evil-minded son of Dhritarashtra.
Bhagavad Gita 1.24 — Sanjaya said: Thus addressed by Gudakesa, O descendant of Bharata! Hrishikesa stationed that excellent chariot between the two armies.
Bhagavad Gita 1.25 — In front of Bhishma and Drona and of all the kings of the earth, and said, 'O son of Pritha! look at these assembled Kauravas.'
Bhagavad Gita 1.26 — There the son of Pritha saw in both armies, fathers and grandfathers, preceptors, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, companions, fathers-in-law, as well as friends.
Bhagavad Gita 1.27 — And seeing all those kinsmen standing (there), the son of Kunti was overcome by excessive pity, and spake thus despondingly.
Bhagavad Gita 1.28 — Arjuna said: Seeing these kinsmen, O Krishna! standing (here) desirous to engage in battle.
Bhagavad Gita 1.29 — My limbs droop down; my mouth is quite dried up; a tremor comes on my body; and my hairs stand on end.
Bhagavad Gita 1.30 — The Gandiva (bow) slips from my hand; my skin burns intensely. I am unable, too, to stand up; my mind whirls round, as it were.
Bhagavad Gita 1.31 — O Kesava! I see adverse omens; and I do not perceive any good (to accrue) after killing (my) kinsmen in the battle.
Bhagavad Gita 1.32 — I do not wish for victory, O Krishna! nor sovereignty, nor pleasures: what is sovereignty to us, O Govinda! what enjoyments, and even life?
Bhagavad Gita 1.33 — Even those, for whose sake we desire sovereignty, enjoyments, and pleasures, are standing here for battle, abandoning life and wealth.
Bhagavad Gita 1.34 — Preceptors, fathers, sons as well as grandfathers, maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, as also (other) relatives.
Bhagavad Gita 1.35 — These I do not wish to kill, though they kill (me), O destroyer of Madhu! even for the sake of sovereignty over the three worlds, how much less then for this earth (alone)?
Bhagavad Gita 1.36 — What joy shall be ours, O Janardana! after killing Dhritarashtra's sons? Killing these felons we shall only incur sin.
Bhagavad Gita 1.37 — Therefore it is not proper for us to kill our own kinsmen, the sons of Dhritarashtra. For how, O Madhava! shall we be happy after killing our own relatives?
Bhagavad Gita 1.38 — Although having their consciences corrupted by avarice, they do not see the evils flowing from the extinction of a family, and the sin in treachery to friends.
Bhagavad Gita 1.39 — Still, O Janardana! should not we, who do see the evils flowing from the extinction of a family, learn to refrain from that sin?
Bhagavad Gita 1.40 — On the extinction of a family, the eternal rites of families are destroyed. Those rites being destroyed, impiety predominates over the whole family.

Bhagavad Gita 1.41 — In consequence of the predominance of impiety, O Krishna! the women of the family become corrupt; and the women becoming corrupt, O descendant of Vrishni! intermingling of castes results.

Bhagavad Gita 1.42 — That intermingling necessarily leads the family and the destroyers of the family to hell; for when the ceremonies of (offering) the balls of food and water (to them) fail, their ancestors fall down (to hell).
Bhagavad Gita 1.43 — By these transgressions of the destroyers of families, which occasion interminglings of castes, the eternal rites of castes and rites, of families are subverted.
Bhagavad Gita 1.44 — And O Janardana! we have heard that men whose family-rites are subverted, must necessarily live in hell.
Bhagavad Gita 1.45 — Alas! we are engaged in committing a heinous sin, seeing that we are making efforts for killing our own kinsmen out of greed of the pleasures of sovereignty.
Bhagavad Gita 1.46 — If the sons of Dhritarashtra, weapon in hand, should kill me in battle, me weaponless and not defending (myself), that would be better for me.
Bhagavad Gita 1.47 — Sanjaya said: Having spoken thus, Arjuna cast aside his bow together with the arrows, on the battle-field, and sat down in (his) chariot, with a mind agitated by grief.
Bhagavad Gita 2.1 — Sanjaya said: To him, who was thus overcome with pity, and dejected, and whose eyes were full of tears and turbid, the destroyer of Madhu spoke these words.

Bhagavad Gita 2.2 — The Deity said: How (comes it that) this delusion, O Arjuna! which is discarded by the good, which excludes from heaven, and occasions infamy, has overtaken you in this (place of) peril?
Bhagavad Gita 2.3 — Be not effeminate, O son of Pritha! it is not worthy of you. Cast off this base weakness of heart, and arise, O terror of (your) foes!
Bhagavad Gita 2.4 — Arjuna said: How, O destroyer of Madhu! shall I encounter with arrows in the battle Bhishma and Drona—both, O destroyer of enemies! entitled to reverence?

Bhagavad Gita 2.5 — Not killing (my) preceptors—(men) of great glory—it is better to live even on alms in this world. But killing them, though they are avaricious of worldly goods, I should only enjoy blood-tainted enjoyments.

Bhagavad Gita 2.6 — Nor do we know which of the two is better for us—whether that we should vanquish them, or that they should vanquish us. Even those, whom having killed, we do not wish to live—even those sons of Dhritarashtra stand (arrayed) against us.

Bhagavad Gita 2.7 — With a heart contaminated by the taint of helplessness, with a mind confounded about my duty, I ask you. Tell me what is assuredly good for me. I am your disciple; instruct me, who have thrown myself on your (indulgence).

Bhagavad Gita 2.8 — For I do not perceive what is to dispel that grief which will dry up my organs after I shall have obtained a prosperous kingdom on earth without a foe, or even the sovereignty of the gods.
Bhagavad Gita 2.9 — Sanjaya said: Having spoken thus to Hrishikesa, O terror of (your) foes! Gudakesa said to Govinda, 'I shall not engage in battle;' and verily remained silent.
Bhagavad Gita 2.10 — To him thus desponding between the two armies, O descendant of Bharata! Hrishikesa spoke these words with a slight smile.
Bhagavad Gita 2.11 — The Deity said: You have grieved for those who deserve no grief, and you talk words of wisdom. Learned men grieve not for the living nor the dead.
Bhagavad Gita 2.12 — Never did I not exist, nor you, nor these rulers of men; nor will any one of us ever hereafter cease to be.
Bhagavad Gita 2.13 — As, in this body, infancy and youth and old age (come) to the embodied (self), so does the acquisition of another body; a sensible man is not deceived about that.
Bhagavad Gita 2.14 — The contacts of the senses, O son of Kunti! which produce cold and heat, pleasure and pain, are not permanent, they are ever coming and going. Bear them, O descendant of Bharata!
Bhagavad Gita 2.15 — For, O chief of men! that sensible man whom they (pain and pleasure being alike to him) afflict not, he merits immortality.

Bhagavad Gita 2.16 — There is no existence for that which is unreal; there is no non-existence for that which is real. And the (correct) conclusion about both is perceived by those who perceive the truth.
Bhagavad Gita 2.17 — Know that to be indestructible which pervades all this; the destruction of that inexhaustible (principle) none can bring about.

Bhagavad Gita 2.18 — These bodies appertaining to the embodied (self) which is eternal, indestructible, and indefinable, are said to be perishable; therefore do engage in battle, O descendant of Bharata!
Bhagavad Gita 2.19 — He who thinks it to be the killer and he who thinks it to be killed, both know nothing. It kills not, is not killed.
Bhagavad Gita 2.20 — It is not born, nor does it ever die, nor, having existed, does it exist no more. Unborn, everlasting, unchangeable, and primeval, it is not killed when the body is killed.
Bhagavad Gita 2.21 — O son of Pritha! how can that man who knows it thus to be indestructible, everlasting, unborn, and inexhaustible, how and whom can he kill, whom can he cause to be killed?
Bhagavad Gita 2.22 — As a man, casting off old clothes, puts on others and new ones, so the embodied (self) casting off old bodies, goes to others and new ones.
Bhagavad Gita 2.23 — Weapons do not divide it (into pieces); fire does not burn it, waters do not moisten it; the wind does not dry it up.
Bhagavad Gita 2.24 — It is not divisible; it is not combustible; it is not to be moistened; it is not to be dried up. It is everlasting, all-pervading, stable, firm, and eternal.
Bhagavad Gita 2.25 — It is said to be unperceived, to be unthinkable, to be unchangeable. Therefore knowing it to be such, you ought not to grieve.
Bhagavad Gita 2.26 — But even if you think that it is constantly born, and constantly dies, still, O you of mighty arms! you ought not to grieve thus.
Bhagavad Gita 2.27 — For to one that is born, death is certain; and to one that dies, birth is certain. Therefore about (this) unavoidable thing, you ought not to grieve.

Bhagavad Gita 2.28 — The source of things, O descendant of Bharata! is unperceived; their middle state is perceived; and their end again is unperceived. What (occasion is there for any) lamentation regarding them?
Bhagavad Gita 2.29 — One looks upon it as a wonder; another similarly speaks of it as a wonder; another too hears of it as a wonder; and even after having heard of it, no one does really know it.
Bhagavad Gita 2.30 — This embodied (self), O descendant of Bharata! within every one's body is ever indestructible. Therefore you ought not to grieve for any being.
Bhagavad Gita 2.31 — Having regard to your own duty also, you ought not to falter, for there is nothing better for a Kshatriya than a righteous battle.
Bhagavad Gita 2.32 — Happy those Kshatriyas, O son of Pritha! who can find such a battle (to fight)—come of itself—an open door to heaven!
Bhagavad Gita 2.33 — But if you will not fight this righteous battle, then you will have abandoned your own duty and your fame, and you will incur sin.
Bhagavad Gita 2.34 — All beings, too, will tell of your everlasting infamy; and to one who has been honoured, infamy is (a) greater (evil) than death.
Bhagavad Gita 2.35 — (Warriors who are) masters of great cars will think that you abstained from the battle through fear, and having been highly thought of by them, you will fall down to littleness.
Bhagavad Gita 2.36 — Your enemies, too, decrying your power, will speak much about you that should not be spoken. And what, indeed, more lamentable than that?
Bhagavad Gita 2.37 — Killed, you will obtain heaven; victorious, you will enjoy the earth. Therefore arise, O son of Kunti! resolved to (engage in) battle.
Bhagavad Gita 2.38 — Looking alike on pleasure and pain, on gain and loss, on victory and defeat, then prepare for battle, and thus you will not incur sin.

Bhagavad Gita 2.39 — The knowledge here declared to you is that relating to the Sankhya. Now hear that relating to the Yoga. Possessed of this knowledge, O son of Pritha! you will cast off the bonds of action.
Bhagavad Gita 2.40 — In this (path to final emancipation) nothing that is commenced becomes abortive; no obstacles exist; and even a little of this (form of) piety protects one from great danger.

Bhagavad Gita 2.41 — There is here, O descendant of Kuru! but one state of mind consisting in firm understanding. But the states of mind of those who have no firm understanding are many-branched and endless.

Bhagavad Gita 2.42 — The state of mind consisting in firm understanding regarding steady contemplation does not belong to those, O son of Pritha! who are strongly attached to (worldly) pleasures and power, and whose minds are drawn away by that flowery talk which is full of (ordinances of) specific acts for the attainment of (those) pleasures and (that) power, and which promises birth as the fruit of acts—(that flowery talk) which those unwise ones utter, who are enamoured of Vedic words, who say there is nothing else, who are full of desires, and whose goal is heaven.

Bhagavad Gita 2.43 — The state of mind consisting in firm understanding regarding steady contemplation does not belong to those, O son of Pritha! who are strongly attached to (worldly) pleasures and power, and whose minds are drawn away by that flowery talk which is full of (ordinances of) specific acts for the attainment of (those) pleasures and (that) power, and which promises birth as the fruit of acts—(that flowery talk) which those unwise ones utter, who are enamoured of Vedic words, who say there is nothing else, who are full of desires, and whose goal is heaven.

Bhagavad Gita 2.44 — The state of mind consisting in firm understanding regarding steady contemplation does not belong to those, O son of Pritha! who are strongly attached to (worldly) pleasures and power, and whose minds are drawn away by that flowery talk which is full of (ordinances of) specific acts for the attainment of (those) pleasures and (that) power, and which promises birth as the fruit of acts—(that flowery talk) which those unwise ones utter, who are enamoured of Vedic words, who say there is nothing else, who are full of desires, and whose goal is heaven.

Bhagavad Gita 2.45 — The Vedas (merely) relate to the effects of the three qualities; do you, O Arjuna! rise above those effects of the three qualities, and be free from the pairs of opposites, always preserve courage, be free from anxiety for new acquisitions or protection of old acquisitions, and be self-controlled.
Bhagavad Gita 2.46 — To the instructed Brahmana, there is in all the Vedas as much utility as in a reservoir of water into which waters flow from all sides.
Bhagavad Gita 2.47 — Your business is with action alone; not by any means with fruit. Let not the fruit of action be your motive (to action). Let not your attachment be (fixed) on inaction.
Bhagavad Gita 2.48 — Having recourse to devotion, O Dhananjaya! perform actions, casting off (all) attachment, and being equable in success or ill-success; (such) equability is called devotion.
Bhagavad Gita 2.49 — Action, O Dhananjaya! is far inferior to the devotion of the mind. In that devotion seek shelter. Wretched are those whose motive (to action) is the fruit (of action).
Bhagavad Gita 2.50 — He who has obtained devotion in this world casts off both merit and sin. Therefore apply yourself to devotion; devotion in (all) actions is wisdom.
Bhagavad Gita 2.51 — The wise who have obtained devotion cast off the fruit of action; and released from the shackles of (repeated) births, repair to that seat where there is no unhappiness.
Bhagavad Gita 2.52 — When your mind shall have crossed beyond the taint of delusion, then will you become indifferent to all that you have heard or will hear.
Bhagavad Gita 2.53 — When your mind, confounded by what you have heard, will stand firm and steady in contemplation, then will you acquire devotion.
Bhagavad Gita 2.54 — Arjuna said: What are the characteristics, O Kesava! of one whose mind is steady, and who is intent on contemplation? How should one of steady mind speak, how sit, how move?
Bhagavad Gita 2.55 — The Deity said: When a man, O son of Pritha! abandons all the desires of his heart, and is pleased in his self only and by his self, he is then called one of steady mind.

Bhagavad Gita 2.56 — He whose heart is not agitated in the midst of calamities, who has no longing for pleasures, and from whom (the feelings of) affection, fear, and wrath have departed, is called a sage of steady mind.
Bhagavad Gita 2.57 — His mind is steady, who, being without attachments anywhere, feels no exultation and no aversion on encountering the various agreeable and disagreeable (things of this world).
Bhagavad Gita 2.58 — A man's mind is steady, when he withdraws his senses from (all) objects of sense, as the tortoise (withdraws) its limbs from all sides.
Bhagavad Gita 2.59 — Objects of sense draw back from a person who is abstinent; not so the taste (for those objects). But even the taste departs from him, when he has seen the Supreme.
Bhagavad Gita 2.60 — The boisterous senses, O son of Kunti! carry away by force the mind even of a wise man, who exerts himself (for final emancipation).
Bhagavad Gita 2.61 — Restraining them all, a man should remain engaged in devotion, making me his only resort. For his mind is steady whose senses are under his control.
Bhagavad Gita 2.62 — The man who ponders over objects of sense forms an attachment to them; from (that) attachment is produced desire; and from desire anger is produced.

Bhagavad Gita 2.63 — From anger results want of discrimination; from want of discrimination, confusion of the memory; from confusion of the memory, loss of reason; and in consequence of loss of reason he is utterly ruined.
Bhagavad Gita 2.64 — But the self-restrained man who moves among objects with senses under the control of his own self, and free from affection and aversion, obtains tranquillity.
Bhagavad Gita 2.65 — When there is tranquillity, all his miseries are destroyed, for the mind of him whose heart is tranquil soon becomes steady.

Bhagavad Gita 2.66 — He who is not self-restrained has no steadiness of mind; nor has he who is not self-restrained perseverance in the pursuit of self-knowledge; there is no tranquillity for him who does not persevere in the pursuit of self-knowledge; and whence can there be happiness for one who is not tranquil?
Bhagavad Gita 2.67 — For the heart which follows the rambling senses leads away his judgment, as the wind leads a boat astray upon the waters.
Bhagavad Gita 2.68 — Therefore, O you of mighty arms! his mind is steady whose senses are restrained on all sides from objects of sense.
Bhagavad Gita 2.69 — The self-restrained man is awake, when it is night for all beings; and when all beings are awake, that is the night of the right-seeing sage.

Bhagavad Gita 2.70 — He into whom all objects of desire enter, as waters enter the ocean, which, (though) replenished, (still) keeps its position unmoved,—he only obtains tranquillity; not he who desires (those) objects of desire.
Bhagavad Gita 2.71 — The man who, casting off all desires, lives free from attachments, who is free from egoism, and from (the feeling that this or that is) mine, obtains tranquillity.
Bhagavad Gita 2.72 — This, O son of Pritha! is the Brahmic state; attaining to this, one is never deluded; and remaining in it in (one's) last moments, one attains (brahma-nirvana) the Brahmic bliss.
Bhagavad Gita 3.1 — Arjuna said: If, O Janardana! devotion is deemed by you to be superior to action, then why, O Kesava! do you prompt me to (this) fearful action?
Bhagavad Gita 3.2 — You seem, indeed, to confuse my mind by equivocal words. Therefore, declare one thing determinately, by which I may attain the highest good.

Bhagavad Gita 3.3 — The Deity said: O sinless one! I have already declared, that in this world there is a twofold path—that of the Sankhyas by devotion in the shape of (true) knowledge; and that of the Yogins by devotion in the shape of action.
Bhagavad Gita 3.4 — A man does not attain freedom from action merely by not engaging in action; nor does he attain perfection by mere renunciation.

Bhagavad Gita 3.5 — For nobody ever remains even for an instant without performing some action; since the qualities of nature constrain everybody, not having free-will (in the matter), to some action.
Bhagavad Gita 3.6 — The deluded man who, restraining the organs of action, continues to think in his mind about objects of sense, is called a hypocrite.

Bhagavad Gita 3.7 — But he, O Arjuna! who restraining his senses by his mind, and being free from attachments, engages in devotion (in the shape) of action, with the organs of action, is far superior.
Bhagavad Gita 3.8 — Do you perform prescribed action, for action is better than inaction, and the support of your body, too, cannot be accomplished with inaction.

Bhagavad Gita 3.9 — This world is fettered by all action other than action for the purpose of the sacrifice. Therefore, O son of Kunti! do you, casting off attachment, perform action for that purpose.
Bhagavad Gita 3.10 — The Creator, having in olden times created men together with the sacrifice, said: Propagate with this. May it be the giver to you of the things you desire.
Bhagavad Gita 3.11 — Please the gods with this, and may those gods please you. Pleasing each other, you will attain the highest good.
Bhagavad Gita 3.12 — For pleased with the sacrifices, the gods will give you the enjoyments you desire. And he who enjoys himself without giving them what they have given, is, indeed, a thief.
Bhagavad Gita 3.13 — The good, who eat the leavings of a sacrifice, are released from all sins. But the unrighteous ones, who prepare food for themselves only, incur sin.
Bhagavad Gita 3.14 — From food are born (all) creatures; from rain is the production of food; rain is produced by sacrifices; sacrifices are the result of action.
Bhagavad Gita 3.15 — Know that action has its source in the Vedas; the Vedas come from the Indestructible. Therefore the all-comprehending Vedas are always concerned with sacrifices.
Bhagavad Gita 3.16 — He who in this world does not turn round the wheel revolving thus, is of sinful life, indulging his senses, and, O son of Pritha! he lives in vain.
Bhagavad Gita 3.17 — But the man who is attached to his self only, who is contented in his self, and is pleased with his self, has nothing to do.
Bhagavad Gita 3.18 — He has no interest at all in what is done, and none whatever in what is not done, in this world; nor is any interest of his dependent on any being.
Bhagavad Gita 3.19 — Therefore always perform action, which must be performed, without attachment. For a man, performing action without attachment, attains the Supreme.
Bhagavad Gita 3.20 — By action alone, did Janaka and the rest work for perfection. And having regard also to the keeping of people (to their duties) you should perform action.
Bhagavad Gita 3.21 — Whatever a great man does, that other men also do. And people follow whatever he receives as authority.
Bhagavad Gita 3.22 — There is nothing, O son of Pritha! for me to do in (all) the three worlds, nothing to acquire which has not been acquired. Still I do engage in action.
Bhagavad Gita 3.23 — For should I at any time not engage without sloth in action, men would follow in my path from all sides, O son of Pritha!
Bhagavad Gita 3.24 — If I did not perform actions, these worlds would be destroyed, I should be the cause of caste interminglings; and I should be ruining these people.
Bhagavad Gita 3.25 — As the ignorant act, O descendant of Bharata! with attachment to action, so should a wise man act without attachment, wishing to keep the people (to their duties).
Bhagavad Gita 3.26 — A wise man should not shake the convictions of the ignorant who are attached to action, but acting with devotion (himself) should make them apply themselves to all action.
Bhagavad Gita 3.27 — He whose mind is deluded by egoism thinks himself the doer of the actions, which, in every way, are done by the qualities of nature.

Bhagavad Gita 3.28 — But he, O you of mighty arms! who knows the truth about the difference from qualities and the difference from actions, forms no attachments, believing that qualities deal with qualities.

Bhagavad Gita 3.29 — But those who are deluded by the qualities of nature form attachments to the actions of the qualities. A man of perfect knowledge should not shake these men of imperfect knowledge (in their convictions).

Bhagavad Gita 3.30 — Dedicating all actions to me with a mind knowing the relation of the supreme and individual self, engage in battle without desire, without (any feeling that this or that is) mine, and without any mental trouble.
Bhagavad Gita 3.31 — Even those men who always act on this opinion of mine, full of faith, and without carping, are released from all actions.
Bhagavad Gita 3.32 — But those who carp at my opinion and do not act upon it, know them to be devoid of discrimination, deluded as regards all knowledge, and ruined.
Bhagavad Gita 3.33 — Even a man of knowledge acts consonantly to his own nature. All beings follow nature. What will restraint effect?
Bhagavad Gita 3.34 — Every sense has its affections and aversions towards its objects fixed. One should not become subject to them, for they are one's opponents.

Bhagavad Gita 3.35 — One's own duty, though defective, is better than another's duty well performed. Death in (performing) one's own duty is preferable; the (performance of the) duty of others is dangerous.
Bhagavad Gita 3.36 — Arjuna said: But by whom, O descendant of Vrishni! is man impelled, even though unwilling, and, as it were, constrained by force, to commit sin?
Bhagavad Gita 3.37 — The Deity said: It is desire, it is wrath, born from the quality of passion; it is very ravenous, very sinful. Know that that is the foe in this world.
Bhagavad Gita 3.38 — As fire is enveloped by smoke, a mirror by dust, the foetus by the womb, so is this enveloped by desire.
Bhagavad Gita 3.39 — Knowledge, O son of Kunti! is enveloped by this constant foe of the man of knowledge, in the shape of desire, which is like a fire and insatiable.
Bhagavad Gita 3.40 — The senses, the mind, and the understanding are said to be its seat; with these it deludes the embodied (self) after enveloping knowledge.
Bhagavad Gita 3.41 — Therefore, O chief of the descendants of Bharata! first restrain your senses, then cast off this sinful thing which destroys knowledge and experience.
Bhagavad Gita 3.42 — It has been said, Great are the senses, greater than the senses is the mind, greater than the mind is the understanding. What is greater than the understanding is that.
Bhagavad Gita 3.43 — Thus knowing that which is higher than the understanding, and restraining (your)self by (your)self, O you of mighty arms! destroy this unmanageable enemy in the shape of desire.
Bhagavad Gita 4.1 — The Deity said: This everlasting (system of) devotion I declared to the sun, the sun declared it to Manu, and Manu communicated it to Ikshvaku.
Bhagavad Gita 4.2 — Coming thus by steps, it became known to royal sages. But, O terror of (your) foes! that devotion was lost to the world by long (lapse of) time.
Bhagavad Gita 4.3 — That same primeval devotion I have declared to you to-day, seeing that you are my devotee and friend, for it is the highest mystery.
Bhagavad Gita 4.4 — Arjuna said: Later is your birth the birth of the sun is prior. How then shall I understand that you declared (this) first?
Bhagavad Gita 4.5 — The Deity said: I have passed through many births, O Arjuna! and you also. I know them all, but you, O terror of (your) foes! do not know them.

Bhagavad Gita 4.6 — Even though I am unborn and inexhaustible in (my) essence, even though I am lord of all beings, still I take up the control of my own nature, and am born by means of my delusive power.
Bhagavad Gita 4.7 — Whensoever, O descendant of Bharata! piety languishes, and impiety is in the ascendant, I create myself.
Bhagavad Gita 4.8 — I am born age after age, for the protection of the good, for the destruction of evil-doers, and the establishment of piety.
Bhagavad Gita 4.9 — Whoever truly knows thus my divine birth and work, casts off (this) body and is not born again. He comes to me, O Arjuna!
Bhagavad Gita 4.10 — Many from whom affection, fear, and wrath have departed, who are full of me, who depend on me, and who are purified by the penance of knowledge, have come into my essence.
Bhagavad Gita 4.11 — I serve men in the way in which they approach me. In every way, O son of Pritha! men follow in my path.
Bhagavad Gita 4.12 — Desiring the success of actions, men in this world worship the divinities, for in this world of mortals, the success produced by action is soon obtained.

Bhagavad Gita 4.13 — The fourfold division of castes was created by me according to the apportionment of qualities and duties. But though I am its author, know me to be inexhaustible, and not the author.
Bhagavad Gita 4.14 — Actions defile me not. I have no attachment to the fruit of actions. He who knows me thus is not tied down by actions.
Bhagavad Gita 4.15 — Knowing this, the men of old who wished for final emancipation, performed action. Therefore do you, too, perform action as was done by men of old in olden times.
Bhagavad Gita 4.16 — Even sages are confused as to what is action, what inaction. Therefore I will speak to you about action, and learning that, you will be freed from (this world of) evil.

Bhagavad Gita 4.17 — One must possess knowledge about action; one must also possess knowledge about prohibited action; and again one must possess knowledge about inaction. The truth regarding action is abstruse.
Bhagavad Gita 4.18 — He is wise among men, he is possessed of devotion, and performs all actions, who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction.
Bhagavad Gita 4.19 — The wise call him learned, whose acts are all free from desires and fancies, and whose actions are burnt down by the fire of knowledge.
Bhagavad Gita 4.20 — Forsaking all attachment to the fruit of action, always contented, dependent on none, he does nothing at all, though he engages in action.
Bhagavad Gita 4.21 — Devoid of expectations, restraining the mind and the self, and casting off all belongings, he incurs no sin, performing actions merely for the sake of the body.

Bhagavad Gita 4.22 — Satisfied with earnings coming spontaneously, rising above the pairs of opposites, free from all animosity, and equable on success or ill-success, he is not fettered down, even though he performs (actions).
Bhagavad Gita 4.23 — The acts of one who is devoid of attachment, who is free, whose mind is fixed on knowledge, and who performs action for (the purpose of) the sacrifice are all destroyed.

Bhagavad Gita 4.24 — Brahman is the oblation; with Brahman (as a sacrificial instrument) it is offered up; Brahman is in the fire; and by Brahman it is thrown; and Brahman, too, is the goal to which he proceeds who meditates on Brahman in the action.
Bhagavad Gita 4.25 — Some devotees perform the sacrifice to the gods, some offer up the sacrifice by the sacrifice itself in the fire of Brahman.

Bhagavad Gita 4.26 — Others offer up the senses, such as the sense of hearing and others, in the fires of restraint; others offer up the objects of sense, such as sound and so forth, into the fires of the senses.
Bhagavad Gita 4.27 — Some again offer up all the operations of the senses and the operations of the life-breaths into the fire of devotion by self-restraint, kindled by knowledge.

Bhagavad Gita 4.28 — Others perform the sacrifice of wealth, the sacrifice of penance, the sacrifice of concentration of mind, the sacrifice of Vedic study, and of knowledge, and others are ascetics of rigid vows.

Bhagavad Gita 4.29 — Some offer up the upward life-breath into the downward life-breath, and the downward life-breath into the upper life-breath, and stopping up the motions of the upward and downward life-breaths, devote themselves to the restraint of the life-breaths.
Bhagavad Gita 4.30 — Others, who (take) limited food, offer up the life-breaths into the life-breaths. All of these, conversant with the sacrifice, have their sins destroyed by the sacrifice.

Bhagavad Gita 4.31 — Those who eat the nectar-like leavings of the sacrifice repair to the eternal Brahman. This world is not for those who perform no sacrifice, whence (then) the other, O best of the Kauravas!
Bhagavad Gita 4.32 — Thus sacrifices of various sorts are laid down in the Vedas. Know them all to be produced from action, and knowing this you will be released (from the fetters of this world).
Bhagavad Gita 4.33 — The sacrifice of knowledge, O terror of (your) foes! is superior to the sacrifice of wealth, for action, O son of Pritha! is wholly and entirely comprehended in knowledge.
Bhagavad Gita 4.34 — That you should learn by salutation, question, and service. The men of knowledge who perceive the truth will teach knowledge to you.
Bhagavad Gita 4.35 — Having learnt that, O son of Pandu! you will not again fall thus into delusion; and by means of it, you will see all beings, without exception, first in yourself, and then in me.
Bhagavad Gita 4.36 — Even if you are the most sinful of all sinful men, you will cross over all trespasses by means of the boat of knowledge alone.
Bhagavad Gita 4.37 — As a fire well kindled, O Arjuna! reduces fuel to ashes, so the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes.
Bhagavad Gita 4.38 — For there is in this world no means of sanctification like knowledge, and that one perfected by devotion finds within one's self in time.
Bhagavad Gita 4.39 — He who has faith, whose senses are restrained, and who is assiduous, obtains knowledge. Obtaining knowledge, he acquires, without delay, the highest tranquillity.
Bhagavad Gita 4.40 — He who is ignorant and devoid of faith, and whose self is full of misgivings, is ruined. Not this world, not the next, nor happiness, is for him whose self is full of misgivings.
Bhagavad Gita 4.41 — Actions, O Dhananjaya! do not fetter one who is self-possessed, who has renounced action by devotion, and who has destroyed misgivings by knowledge.

Bhagavad Gita 4.42 — Therefore, O descendant of Bharata! destroy, with the sword of knowledge, these misgivings of yours which fill your mind, and which are produced from ignorance. Engage in devotion. Arise!
Bhagavad Gita 5.1 — Arjuna said: O Krishna! you praise renunciation of actions and also the pursuit (of them). Tell me determinately which one of these two is superior.
Bhagavad Gita 5.2 — The Deity said: Renunciation and pursuit of action are both instruments of happiness. But of the two, pursuit of action is superior to renunciation of action.

Bhagavad Gita 5.3 — He should be understood to be always an ascetic, who has no aversion and no desire. For, O you of mighty arms! he who is free from the pairs of opposites is easily released from (all) bonds.
Bhagavad Gita 5.4 — Children—not wise men—talk of sankhya and yoga as distinct. One who pursues either well obtains the fruit of both.
Bhagavad Gita 5.5 — The seat which the sankhyas obtain is reached by the yogas also. He sees (truly), who sees the sankhya and yoga as one.
Bhagavad Gita 5.6 — Renunciation, O you of mighty arms! is difficult to reach without devotion; the sage possessed of devotion attains Brahman without delay.

Bhagavad Gita 5.7 — He who is possessed of devotion, whose self is pure, who has restrained his self, and who has controlled his senses, and who identifies his self with every being, is not tainted though he performs (actions).
Bhagavad Gita 5.8 — The man of devotion, who knows the truth, thinks he does nothing at all, when he sees, hears, touches, smells, eats, moves, sleeps, breathes.
Bhagavad Gita 5.9 — Talks, throws out, takes, opens or closes the eyelids; he holds that the senses deal with the objects of the senses.
Bhagavad Gita 5.10 — He who, casting off (all) attachment, performs actions dedicating them to Brahman, is not tainted by sin, as the lotus-leaf (is not tainted) by water.
Bhagavad Gita 5.11 — Devotees, casting off attachment, perform actions for attaining purity of self, with the body, the mind, the understanding, or even the senses—(all) free (from egoistic notions).

Bhagavad Gita 5.12 — He who is possessed of devotion, abandoning the fruit of actions, attains the highest tranquillity. He who is without devotion, and attached to the fruit (of action), is tied down by (reason of his) acting in consequence of (some) desire.
Bhagavad Gita 5.13 — The self-restrained, embodied (self) lies at ease within the city of nine portals, renouncing all actions by the mind, not doing nor causing (any thing) to be done.
Bhagavad Gita 5.14 — The Lord is not the cause of actions, or of the capacity of performing actions amongst men, or of the connexion of action and fruit. But nature only works.
Bhagavad Gita 5.15 — The Lord receives no one's sin, nor merit either. Knowledge is enveloped by ignorance, hence all creatures are deluded.
Bhagavad Gita 5.16 — But to those who have destroyed that ignorance by knowledge of the self, (such) knowledge, like the sun, shows forth that supreme (principle).

Bhagavad Gita 5.17 — And those whose mind is (centred) on it, whose (very) self it is, who are thoroughly devoted to it, and whose final goal it is, go never to return, having their sins destroyed by knowledge.
Bhagavad Gita 5.18 — The wise look upon a Brahmana possessed of learning and humility, on a cow, an elephant, a dog, and a Svapaka, as alike.
Bhagavad Gita 5.19 — Even here, those have conquered the material world, whose mind rests in equability; since Brahman is free from defects and equable, therefore they rest in Brahman.

Bhagavad Gita 5.20 — He who knows Brahman, whose mind is steady, who is not deluded, and who rests in Brahman, does not exult on finding anything agreeable, nor does he grieve on finding anything disagreeable.

Bhagavad Gita 5.21 — One whose self is not attached to external objects, obtains the happiness that is in (one's) self; and by means of concentration of mind, joining one's self (with the Brahman), one obtains indestructible happiness.

Bhagavad Gita 5.22 — For the enjoyments born of contact (between senses and their objects) are, indeed, sources of misery; they have a beginning as well as an end. O son of Kunti! a wise man feels no pleasure in them.
Bhagavad Gita 5.23 — He who even in this world, before his release from the body, is able to bear the agitations produced from desire and wrath, is a devoted man, he is a happy man.

Bhagavad Gita 5.24 — The devotee whose happiness is within (himself), whose recreation is within (himself), and whose light (of knowledge) also is within (himself), becoming (one with) the Brahman, obtain the Brahmic bliss.
Bhagavad Gita 5.25 — The sages whose sins have perished, whose misgivings are destroyed, who are self-restrained, and who are intent on the welfare of all beings, obtain the Brahmic bliss.
Bhagavad Gita 5.26 — To the ascetics, who are free from desire and wrath, and whose minds are restrained, and who have knowledge of the self, the Brahmic bliss is on both sides (of death).

Bhagavad Gita 5.27 — The sage who excludes (from his mind) external objects, (concentrates) the visual power between the brows, and making the upward and downward life-breaths even, confines their movements within the nose.

Bhagavad Gita 5.28 — Who restrains senses, mind, and understanding, whose highest goal is final emancipation, from whom desire, fear, and wrath have departed, is, indeed, for ever released (from birth and death).
Bhagavad Gita 5.29 — He knowing me to be the enjoyer of all sacrifices and penances, the great Lord of all worlds, and the friend of all beings, attains tranquillity.

Bhagavad Gita 6.1 — The Deity said: He who, regardless of the fruit of actions, performs the actions which ought to be performed, is the devotee and renouncer; not he who discards the (sacred) fires, nor he who performs no acts.
Bhagavad Gita 6.2 — Know, O son of Pandu! that what is called renunciation is devotion; for nobody becomes a devotee who has not renounced (all) fancies.
Bhagavad Gita 6.3 — To the sage who wishes to rise to devotion, action is said to be a means, and to him, when he has risen to devotion, tranquillity is said to be a means.
Bhagavad Gita 6.4 — When one does not attach oneself to objects of sense, nor to action, renouncing all fancies, then is one said to have risen to devotion.
Bhagavad Gita 6.5 — (A man) should elevate his self by his self; he should not debase his self, for even (a man's) own self is his friend, (a man's) own self is also his enemy.
Bhagavad Gita 6.6 — To him who has subjugated his self by his self, his self is a friend; but to him who has not restrained his self, his own self behaves inimically, like an enemy.

Bhagavad Gita 6.7 — The self of one who has subjugated his self and is tranquil, is absolutely concentrated (on itself), in the midst of cold and heat, pleasure and pain, as well as honour and dishonour.

Bhagavad Gita 6.8 — The devotee whose self is contented with knowledge and experience, who is unmoved, who has restrained his senses, and to whom a sod, a stone, and gold are alike, is said to be devoted.

Bhagavad Gita 6.9 — And he is esteemed highest, who thinks alike about well-wishers, friends, and enemies, and those who are indifferent, and those who take part with both sides, and those who are objects of hatred, and relatives, as well as about the good and the sinful.
Bhagavad Gita 6.10 — A devotee should constantly devote his self to abstraction, remaining in a secret place, alone, with his mind and self restrained, without expectations, and without belongings.
Bhagavad Gita 6.11 — Fixing his seat firmly in a clean place, not too high nor too low, and covered over with a sheet of cloth, a deerskin, and (blades of) Kusa (grass)
Bhagavad Gita 6.12 — And there seated on (that) seat, fixing his mind exclusively on one point, with the workings of the mind and senses restrained, he should practice devotion for purity of self.
Bhagavad Gita 6.13 — Holding his body, head, and neck even and unmoved, (remaining) steady, looking at the tip of his own nose, and not looking about in (all) directions.

Bhagavad Gita 6.14 — With a tranquil self, devoid of fear, and adhering to the rules of Brahmacharins, he should restrain his mind, and (concentrate it) on me, and sit down engaged in devotion, regarding me as his final goal.
Bhagavad Gita 6.15 — Thus constantly devoting his self to abstraction, a devotee whose mind is restrained, attains that tranquillity which culminates in final emancipation, and assimilation with me.
Bhagavad Gita 6.16 — Devotion is not his, O Arjuna! who eats too much, nor his who eats not at all; not his who is addicted to too much sleep, nor his who is (ever) awake.
Bhagavad Gita 6.17 — That devotion which destroys (all) misery is his, who takes due food and exercise, who toils duly in all works, and who sleeps and awakes (in) due (time).
Bhagavad Gita 6.18 — When (a man's) mind well restrained becomes steady upon the self alone, then he being indifferent to all objects of desire, is said to be devoted.
Bhagavad Gita 6.19 — As a light standing in a windless (place) flickers not, that is declared to be the parallel for a devotee, whose mind is restrained, and who devotes his self to abstraction.
Bhagavad Gita 6.20 — That (mental condition), in which the mind restrained by practice of abstraction, ceases to work; in which too, one seeing the self by the self, is pleased in the self.

Bhagavad Gita 6.21 — In which one experiences that infinite happiness which transcends the senses, and which can be grasped by the understanding only; and adhering to which, one never swerves from the truth.
Bhagavad Gita 6.22 — [That state,] acquiring which, one thinks no other acquisition higher than it; and adhering to which, one is not shaken off even by great misery.

Bhagavad Gita 6.23 — That should be understood to be called devotion in which there is a severance of all connexion with pain. That devotion should be practised with steadiness and with an undesponding heart.
Bhagavad Gita 6.24 — Abandoning, without exception, all desires, which are produced from fancies, and restraining the whole group of the senses on all sides by the mind only.
Bhagavad Gita 6.25 — One should by slow steps become quiescent, with a firm resolve coupled with courage; and fixing his mind upon the self, should think of nothing.
Bhagavad Gita 6.26 — Wherever the active and unsteady mind breaks forth, there one should ever restrain it, and fix it steadily on the self alone.

Bhagavad Gita 6.27 — The highest happiness comes to such a devotee, whose mind is fully tranquil, in whom the quality of passion has been suppressed, who is free from sin, and who is become (one with) the Brahman.
Bhagavad Gita 6.28 — Thus constantly devoting his self to abstraction, a devotee, freed from sin, easily obtains that supreme happiness—contact with the Brahman.
Bhagavad Gita 6.29 — He who has devoted his self to abstraction, by devotion, looking alike on everything, sees the self abiding in all beings, and all beings in the self.
Bhagavad Gita 6.30 — To him who sees me in everything, and everything in me, I am never lost, and he is not lost to me.
Bhagavad Gita 6.31 — The devotee who worships me abiding in all beings, holding that all is one, lives in me, however he may be living.
Bhagavad Gita 6.32 — That devotee, O Arjuna! is deemed to be the best, who looks alike on pleasure or pain, whatever it may be, in all (creatures), comparing all with his own (pleasure or pain).

Bhagavad Gita 6.33 — Arjuna said: I cannot see, O destroyer of Madhu! (how) the sustained existence (is to be secured) of this devotion by means of equanimity which you have declared—in consequence of fickleness.
Bhagavad Gita 6.34 — For, O Krishna! the mind is fickle, boisterous, strong, and obstinate; and I think that to restrain it is as difficult as (to restrain) the wind.

Bhagavad Gita 6.35 — The Deity said: Doubtless, O you of mighty arms! the mind is difficult to restrain, and fickle. Still, O son of Kunti! it may be restrained by constant practice and by indifference (to worldly objects).

Bhagavad Gita 6.36 — It is my belief, that devotion is hard to obtain for one who does not restrain his self. But by one who is self-restrained and assiduous, it can be obtained through (proper) expedients.

Bhagavad Gita 6.37 — Arjuna said: What is the end of him, O Krishna! who does not attain the consummation of his devotion, being not assiduous, and having a mind shaken off from devotion, (though) full of faith?
Bhagavad Gita 6.38 — Does he, fallen from both (paths), go to ruin like a broken cloud, being, O you of mighty arms! without support, and deluded on the path (leading) to the Brahman?
Bhagavad Gita 6.39 — Be pleased, O Krishna! to entirely destroy this doubt of mine, for none else than you can destroy this doubt.
Bhagavad Gita 6.40 — The Deity said: O son of Pritha! neither in this world nor the next, is ruin for him; for, O dear friend! none who performs good (deeds) comes to an evil end.

Bhagavad Gita 6.41 — He who is fallen from devotion attains the worlds of those who perform meritorious acts, dwells (there) for many a year, and is afterwards born into a family of holy and illustrious men.
Bhagavad Gita 6.42 — Or he is even born into a family of talented devotees; for such a birth as that in this world is more difficult to obtain.
Bhagavad Gita 6.43 — There he comes into contact with the knowledge which belonged to him in his former body, and then again, O descendant of Kuru! he works for perfection.

Bhagavad Gita 6.44 — For even though reluctant, he is led away by the self-same former practice, and although he only wishes to learn devotion, he rises above the (fruits of action laid down in the) divine word.
Bhagavad Gita 6.45 — But the devotee working with great efforts, and cleared of his sins, attains perfection after many births, and then reaches the supreme goal.

Bhagavad Gita 6.46 — The devotee is esteemed higher than the performers of penances, higher even than the men of knowledge, and the devotee is higher than the men of action; therefore, O Arjuna! become a devotee.
Bhagavad Gita 6.47 — And even among all devotees, he who, being full of faith, worships me, with his inmost self intent on me, is esteemed by me to be the most devoted.
Bhagavad Gita 7.1 — The Deity said: O son of Pritha! now hear how you can without doubt know me fully, fixing your mind on me, and resting in me, and practising devotion.
Bhagavad Gita 7.2 — I will now tell you exhaustively about knowledge together with experience; that being known, there is nothing further left in this world to know.
Bhagavad Gita 7.3 — Among thousands of men, only some work for perfection; and even of those who have reached perfection, and who are assiduous, only some know me truly.
Bhagavad Gita 7.4 — Earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, understanding, and egoism, thus is my nature divided eightfold.

Bhagavad Gita 7.5 — But this is a lower (form of my) nature. Know (that there is) another (form of my) nature, and higher than this, which is animate, O you of mighty arms! and by which this universe is upheld.
Bhagavad Gita 7.6 — Know that all things have these (for their) source. I am the producer and the destroyer of the whole universe.
Bhagavad Gita 7.7 — There is nothing else, O Dhananjaya! higher than myself; all this is woven upon me, like numbers of pearls upon a thread.
Bhagavad Gita 7.8 — I am the taste in water, O son of Kunti! I am the light of the sun and moon. I am 'Om' in all the Vedas, sound in space, and manliness in human beings.
Bhagavad Gita 7.9 — I am the fragrant smell in the earth, refulgence in the fire; I am life in all beings, and penance in those who perform penance.
Bhagavad Gita 7.10 — Know me, O son of Pritha! to be the eternal seed of all beings; I am the discernment of the discerning ones, and I the glory of the glorious.
Bhagavad Gita 7.11 — I am also the strength, unaccompanied by fondness or desire, of the strong. And, O chief of the descendants of Bharata! I am love unopposed to piety among all beings.

Bhagavad Gita 7.12 — And all entities which are of the quality of goodness, and those which are of the quality of passion and of darkness, know that they are, indeed, all from me; I am not in them, but they are in me.
Bhagavad Gita 7.13 — The whole universe deluded by these three states of mind, developed from the qualities, does not know me, who am beyond them and inexhaustible.
Bhagavad Gita 7.14 — For this delusion of mine, developed from the qualities, is divine and difficult to transcend. Those cross beyond this delusion who resort to me alone.
Bhagavad Gita 7.15 — Wicked men, doers of evil (acts), who are deluded, who are deprived of their knowledge by (this) delusion, and who incline to the demoniac state of mind, do not resort to me.

Bhagavad Gita 7.16 — But, O Arjuna! doers of good (acts) of four classes worship me: one who is distressed, one who is seeking after knowledge, one who wants wealth, and one, O chief of the descendants of Bharata! who is possessed of knowledge.

Bhagavad Gita 7.17 — Of these, he who is possessed of knowledge, who is always devoted, and whose worship is (addressed) to one (Being) only, is esteemed highest. For to the man of knowledge I am dear above all things, and he is dear to me.

Bhagavad Gita 7.18 — All these are noble. But the man possessed of knowledge is deemed by me to be my own self. For he with (his) self devoted to abstraction, has taken to me as the goal than which there is nothing higher.
Bhagavad Gita 7.19 — At the end of many lives, the man possessed of knowledge approaches me, (believing) that Vasudeva is everything. Such a high-souled man is very hard to find.
Bhagavad Gita 7.20 — Those who are deprived of knowledge by various desires approach other divinities, observing various regulations, and controlled by their own natures.
Bhagavad Gita 7.21 — Whichever form (of deity) any worshipper wishes to worship with faith, to that form I render his faith steady.
Bhagavad Gita 7.22 — Possessed of that faith, he seeks to propitiate (the deity in) that (form), and obtains from it those beneficial things which he desires, (though they are) really given by me.
Bhagavad Gita 7.23 — But the fruit thus (obtained) by them, who have little judgment, is perishable. Those who worship the divinities go to the divinities, and my worshippers, too, go to me.
Bhagavad Gita 7.24 — The undiscerning ones, not knowing my transcendent and inexhaustible essence, than which there is nothing higher, think me, who am unperceived, to have become perceptible.
Bhagavad Gita 7.25 — Surrounded by the delusion of my mystic power, I am not manifest to all. This deluded world knows not me unborn and inexhaustible.
Bhagavad Gita 7.26 — I know, O Arjuna! the things which have been, those which are, and those which are to be. But me nobody knows.
Bhagavad Gita 7.27 — All beings, O terror of (your) foes! are deluded at the time of birth by the delusion, O descendant of Bharata! caused by the pairs of opposites arising from desire and aversion.
Bhagavad Gita 7.28 — But the men of meritorious actions, whose sins have terminated, worship me, being released from the delusion (caused) by the pairs of opposites, and being firm in their beliefs.
Bhagavad Gita 7.29 — Those who, resting on me, work for release from old age and death, know the Brahman, the whole Adhyatma, and all action.
Bhagavad Gita 7.30 — And those who know me with the Adhibhuta, the Adhidaiva, and the Adhiyajna, having minds devoted to abstraction, know me at the time of departure (from this world).
Bhagavad Gita 8.1 — Arjuna said: What is that Brahman, what the Adhyatma, and what, O best of beings! is action? And what is called the Adhibhuta?

Bhagavad Gita 8.2 — And who is the Adhiyajna, and how in this body, O destroyer of Madhu? And how, too, are you to be known at the time of departure (from this world) by those who restrain their selfs?

Bhagavad Gita 8.3 — The Deity said: The Brahman is the supreme, the indestructible. Its manifestation (as an individual self) is called the Adhyatma. The offering (of an oblation to any divinity), which is the cause of the production and development of all things, is named action.
Bhagavad Gita 8.4 — The Adhibhuta is all perishable things. The Adhidaivata is the (primal) being. And the Adhiyajna, O best of embodied (beings)! is I myself in this body.
Bhagavad Gita 8.5 — And he who leaves this body and departs (from this world) remembering me in (his) last moments, comes into my essence. There is no doubt of that.
Bhagavad Gita 8.6 — Also whichever form (of deity) he remembers when he finally leaves this body, to that he goes, O son of Kunti! having been used to ponder on it.
Bhagavad Gita 8.7 — Therefore, at all times remember me, and engage in battle. Fixing your mind and understanding on me, you will come to me, there is no doubt.

Bhagavad Gita 8.8 — He who thinks of the supreme divine Being, O son of Pritha! with a mind not (running) to other (objects), and possessed of abstraction in the shape of continuous meditation (about the supreme), goes to him.

Bhagavad Gita 8.9 — He who, possessed of reverence (for the supreme Being) with a steady mind, and with the power of devotion, properly concentrates the life-breath between the brows, and meditates on the ancient Seer, the ruler, more minute than the minutest atom, the supporter of all, who is of an unthinkable form, whose brilliance is like that of the sun, and who is beyond all darkness, he attains to that transcendent and divine Being.

Bhagavad Gita 8.10 — He who, possessed of reverence (for the supreme Being) with a steady mind, and with the power of devotion, properly concentrates the life-breath between the brows, and meditates on the ancient Seer, the ruler, more minute than the minutest atom, the supporter of all, who is of an unthinkable form, whose brilliance is like that of the sun, and who is beyond all darkness, he attains to that transcendent and divine Being.

Bhagavad Gita 8.11 — I will tell you briefly about the seat, which those who know the Vedas declare to be indestructible; which entered by ascetics from whom all desires have departed; and wishing for which, people pursue the mode of life of Brahmacharins.

Bhagavad Gita 8.12 — He who leaves the body and departs (from this world), stopping up all passages, and confining the mind within the heart, placing the life-breath in the head, and adhering to uninterrupted meditation.
Bhagavad Gita 8.13 — Repeating the single syllable 'Om,' (signifying) the eternal Brahman, and meditating on me, he reaches the highest goal.

Bhagavad Gita 8.14 — To the devotee who constantly practises abstraction, O son of Pritha! and who with a mind not (turned) to anything else, is ever and constantly meditating on me, I am easy of access.
Bhagavad Gita 8.15 — The high-souled ones, who achieve the highest perfection, attaining to me, do not again come to life, which is transient, a home of woes.
Bhagavad Gita 8.16 — All worlds, O Arjuna! up to the world of Brahman, are (destined) to return. But, O son of Kunti! after attaining to me, there is no birth again.
Bhagavad Gita 8.17 — Those who know a day of Brahman to end after one thousand ages, and the night to terminate after one thousand ages, are the persons who know day and night.
Bhagavad Gita 8.18 — On the advent of day, all perceptible things are produced from the unperceived; and on the advent of night they dissolve in that same (principle) called the unperceived.

Bhagavad Gita 8.19 — This same assemblage of entities, being produced again and again, dissolves on the advent of night, and, O son of Pritha! issues forth on the advent of day, without a will of its own.
Bhagavad Gita 8.20 — But there is another entity, unperceived and eternal, and distinct from this unperceived (principle), which is not destroyed when all entities are destroyed.
Bhagavad Gita 8.21 — It is called the unperceived, the indestructible; they call it the highest goal. Attaining to it, none returns. That is my supreme abode.
Bhagavad Gita 8.22 — That supreme Being, O son of Pritha! he in whom all these entities dwell, and by whom all this is permeated, is to be attained to by reverence not (directed) to another.
Bhagavad Gita 8.23 — I will state the times, O descendant of Bharata! at which devotees departing (from this world) go, never to return, or to return.
Bhagavad Gita 8.24 — The fire, the flame, the day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the northern solstice, departing (from the world) in these, those who know the Brahman go to the Brahman.
Bhagavad Gita 8.25 — Smoke, night, the dark fortnight, the six months of the southern solstice, (dying) in these, the devotee goes to the lunar light and returns.
Bhagavad Gita 8.26 — These two paths, bright and dark, are deemed to be eternal in this world. By the one, (a man) goes never to return, by the other he comes back.
Bhagavad Gita 8.27 — Knowing these two paths, O son of Pritha! no devotee is deluded. Therefore at all times be possessed of devotion, O Arjuna!

Bhagavad Gita 8.28 — A devotee knowing all this, obtains all the holy fruit which is prescribed for (study of) the Vedas, for sacrifices, and also for penances and gifts, and he attains to the highest and primeval seat.
Bhagavad Gita 9.1 — Now I will speak to you, who are not given to carping, of that most mysterious knowledge, accompanied by experience, by knowing which you will be released from evil.

Bhagavad Gita 9.2 — It is the chief among the sciences, the chief among the mysteries. It is the best means of sanctification. It is imperishable, not opposed to the sacred law. It is to be apprehended directly, and is easy to practise.
Bhagavad Gita 9.3 — O terror of your foes! those men who have no faith in this holy doctrine, return to the path of this mortal world, without attaining to me.
Bhagavad Gita 9.4 — This whole universe is pervaded by me in an unperceived form. All entities live in me, but I do not live in them.
Bhagavad Gita 9.5 — Nor yet do all entities live in me. See my divine power. Supporting all entities and producing all entities, my self lives not in (those) entities.
Bhagavad Gita 9.6 — As the great and ubiquitous atmosphere always remains in space, know that similarly all entities live in me.
Bhagavad Gita 9.7 — At the expiration of a Kalpa, O son of Kunti! all entities enter my nature; and at the beginning of a Kalpa, I again bring them forth.
Bhagavad Gita 9.8 — Taking the control of my own nature, I bring forth again and again this whole collection of entities, without a will of its own, by the power of nature.
Bhagavad Gita 9.9 — But, O Arjuna! these actions do not fetter me, who remain like one unconcerned, and who am unattached to those actions.
Bhagavad Gita 9.10 — Nature gives birth to movables and immovables through me, the supervisor, and by reason of that, O son of Kunti! the universe revolves.

Bhagavad Gita 9.11 — Deluded people of vain hopes, vain acts, vain knowledge, whose minds are disordered, and who are inclined to the delusive nature of Asuras and Rakshasas, not knowing my highest nature as great lord of all entities, disregard me as I have assumed a human body.

Bhagavad Gita 9.12 — Deluded people of vain hopes, vain acts, vain knowledge, whose minds are disordered, and who are inclined to the delusive nature of Asuras and Rakshasas, not knowing my highest nature as great lord of all entities, disregard me as I have assumed a human body.

Bhagavad Gita 9.13 — But the high-souled ones, O son of Pritha! who are inclined to the godlike nature, knowing me as the inexhaustible source of (all) entities, worship me with minds not (turned) elsewhere.
Bhagavad Gita 9.14 — Constantly glorifying me, and exerting themselves, firm in their vows, and saluting me with reverence, they worship me, being always devoted.
Bhagavad Gita 9.15 — And others again, offering up the sacrifice of knowledge, worship me as one, as distinct, and as all-pervading in numerous forms.
Bhagavad Gita 9.16 — I am the Kratu, I am the Yajna, I am the Svadha, I the product of the herbs. I am the sacred verse. I too am the sacrificial butter, and I the fire, I the offering.
Bhagavad Gita 9.17 — I am the father of this universe, the mother, the creator, the grandsire, the thing to be known, the means of sanctification, the syllable Om, the Rik, Saman, and Yajus also.

Bhagavad Gita 9.18 — The goal, the sustainer, the lord, the supervisor, the residence, the asylum, the friend, the source, and that in which it merges, the support, the receptacle, and the inexhaustible seed.
Bhagavad Gita 9.19 — I cause heat and I send forth and stop showers. I am immortality and also death; and I, O Arjuna! am that which is and that which is not.

Bhagavad Gita 9.20 — Those who know the three (branches of) knowledge, who drink the Soma juice, whose sins are washed away, offer sacrifices and pray to me for a passage into heaven; and reaching the holy world of the lord of gods, they enjoy in the celestial regions the celestial pleasures of the gods.

Bhagavad Gita 9.21 — And having enjoyed that great heavenly world, they enter the mortal world when (their) merit is exhausted. Thus those who wish for objects of desire, and resort to the ordinances of the three (Vedas), obtain (as the fruit) going and coming.
Bhagavad Gita 9.22 — To those men who worship me, meditating on me and on no one else, and who are constantly devoted, I give new gifts and preserve what is acquired by them.
Bhagavad Gita 9.23 — Even those, O son of Kunti! who being devotees of other divinities worship with faith, worship me only, (but) irregularly.
Bhagavad Gita 9.24 — For I am the enjoyer as well as the lord of all sacrifices. But they know me not truly, therefore do they fall.

Bhagavad Gita 9.25 — Those who make vows to the gods go to the gods; those who make vows to the manes go to the manes, those who worship the Bhutas go to the Bhutas; and those likewise who worship me go to me.
Bhagavad Gita 9.26 — Whoever with devotion offers me leaf, flower, fruit, water, that, presented with devotion, I accept from him whose self is pure.
Bhagavad Gita 9.27 — Whatever you do, O son of Kunti! whatever you eat, whatever sacrifice you make, whatever you give, whatever penance you perform, do that as offered to me.

Bhagavad Gita 9.28 — Thus will you be released from the bonds of action, the fruits of which are agreeable or disagreeable. And with your self possessed of (this) devotion, (this) renunciation, you will be released (from the bonds of action) and will come to me.
Bhagavad Gita 9.29 — I am alike to all beings; to me none is hateful, none dear. But those who worship me with devotion (dwell) in me, and I too in them.
Bhagavad Gita 9.30 — Even if a very ill-conducted man worships me, not worshipping any one else, he must certainly be deemed to be good, for he has well resolved.
Bhagavad Gita 9.31 — He soon becomes devout of heart, and obtains lasting tranquillity. (You may) affirm, O son of Kunti! that my devotee is never ruined.
Bhagavad Gita 9.32 — For, O son of Pritha! even those who are of sinful birth, women, Vaisyas, and Sudras likewise, resorting to me, attain the supreme goal.
Bhagavad Gita 9.33 — What then (need be said of) holy Brahmanas and royal saints who are (my) devotees? Coming to this transient unhappy world, worship me.

Bhagavad Gita 9.34 — (Place your) mind on me, become my devotee, my worshipper; reverence me, and thus making me your highest goal, and devoting your self to abstraction, you will certainly come to me.
Bhagavad Gita 10.1 — Yet again, O you of mighty arms! listen to my excellent words, which, out of a wish for your welfare, I speak to you who are delighted (with them).
Bhagavad Gita 10.2 — Not the multitudes of gods, nor the great sages know my source; for I am in every way the origin of the gods and great sages.
Bhagavad Gita 10.3 — Of (all) mortals, he who knows me to be unborn, without beginning, the great lord of the world, being free from delusion, is released from all sins.
Bhagavad Gita 10.4 — Intelligence, knowledge, freedom from delusion, forgiveness, truth, restraint of the senses, tranquillity, pleasure, pain, birth, death, fear, and also security.
Bhagavad Gita 10.5 — Harmlessness, equability, contentment, penance, (making) gifts, glory, disgrace, all these different tempers of living beings are from me alone.
Bhagavad Gita 10.6 — The seven great sages, and likewise the four ancient Manus, whose descendants are (all) these people in the world, were all born from my mind, (partaking) of my powers.
Bhagavad Gita 10.7 — Whoever correctly knows these powers and emanations of mine, becomes possessed of devotion free from indecision; of this (there is) no doubt.
Bhagavad Gita 10.8 — The wise, full of love, worship me, believing that I am the origin of all, and that all moves on through me.
Bhagavad Gita 10.9 — (Placing their) minds on me, offering (their) lives to me, instructing each other, and speaking about me, they are always contented and happy.
Bhagavad Gita 10.10 — To these, who are constantly devoted, and who worship with love, I give that knowledge by which they attain to me.
Bhagavad Gita 10.11 — And remaining in their hearts, I destroy, with the brilliant lamp of knowledge, the darkness born of ignorance in such (men) only, out of compassion for them.
Bhagavad Gita 10.12 — Arjuna said: You are the supreme Brahman, the supreme goal, the holiest of the holy.

Bhagavad Gita 10.13 — All sages, as well as the divine sage Narada, Asita, Devala, and Vyasa, call you the eternal being, divine, the first god, the unborn, the all-pervading. And so, too, you tell me yourself, O Kesava!
Bhagavad Gita 10.14 — I believe all this that you tell me (to be) true; for, O lord! neither the gods nor demons understand your manifestation.
Bhagavad Gita 10.15 — You only know your self by your self. O best of beings! creator of all things! lord of all things! god of gods! lord of the universe!
Bhagavad Gita 10.16 — Be pleased to declare without exception your divine emanations, by which emanations you stand pervading all these worlds.
Bhagavad Gita 10.17 — How shall I know you, O you of mystic power! always meditating on you? And in what various entities, O lord! should I meditate on you?
Bhagavad Gita 10.18 — Again, O Janardana! do you yourself declare your powers and emanations; because hearing this nectar, I (still) feel no satiety.
Bhagavad Gita 10.19 — The Deity said: Well then, O best of Kauravas! I will state to you my own divine emanations; but (only) the chief (ones), for there is no end to the extent of my (emanations).
Bhagavad Gita 10.20 — I am the self, O Gudakesa! seated in the hearts of all beings. I am the beginning and the middle and the end also of all beings.
Bhagavad Gita 10.21 — I am Vishnu among the Adityas, the beaming sun among the shining (bodies); I am Marichi among the Maruts, and the moon among the lunar mansions.
Bhagavad Gita 10.22 — Among the Vedas, I am the Sama-veda. I am Indra among the gods. And I am mind among the senses. I am consciousness in (living) beings.
Bhagavad Gita 10.23 — And I am Sankara among the Rudras, the lord of wealth among Yakshas and Rakshasas. And I am fire among the Vasus, and Meru among the high-topped (mountains).
Bhagavad Gita 10.24 — And know me, O Arjuna! to be Brihaspati, the chief among domestic priests. I am Skanda among generals. I am the ocean among reservoirs of water.
Bhagavad Gita 10.25 — I am Bhrigu among the great sages. I am the single syllable (Om) among words. Among sacrifices I am the Japa sacrifice; the Himalaya among the firmly-fixed (mountains)
Bhagavad Gita 10.26 — The Asvattha among all trees, and Narada among divine sages; Chitraratha among the heavenly choristers, the sage Kapila among the Siddhas.
Bhagavad Gita 10.27 — Among horses know me to be Uchchaihsravas, brought forth by (the labours for) the nectar; and Airavata among the great elephants, and the ruler of men among men.
Bhagavad Gita 10.28 — I am the thunderbolt among weapons, the wish-giving (cow) among cows. And I am love which generates. Among serpents I am Vasuki.
Bhagavad Gita 10.29 — Among Naga snakes I am Ananta; I am Varuna among aquatic beings. And I am Aryaman among the manes, and Yama among rulers.
Bhagavad Gita 10.30 — Among demons, too, I am Prahlada. I am the king of death (Kala, time) among those that count. Among beasts I am the lord of beasts, and the son of Vinata among birds.
Bhagavad Gita 10.31 — I am the wind among those that blow. I am Rama among those that wield weapons. Among fishes I am Makara, and among streams the Jahnavi.
Bhagavad Gita 10.32 — Of created things I am the beginning and the end and the middle also, O Arjuna! Among sciences, I am the science of the Adhyatma, and I am the argument of controversialists.
Bhagavad Gita 10.33 — Among letters I am the letter A, and among the group of compounds the copulative compound. I myself am time inexhaustible, and I the creator whose faces are in all directions.
Bhagavad Gita 10.34 — I am death who seizes all, and the source of what is to be. And among females, fame, fortune, speech, memory, intellect, courage, forgiveness.
Bhagavad Gita 10.35 — Likewise among Saman hymns, I am the Brihat-saman, and I the Gayatri among metres. I am Margasirsha among the months, the spring among the seasons.
Bhagavad Gita 10.36 — Of cheats, I am the game of dice; I am the glory of the glorious, I am victory, I am industry, I am the goodness of the good.
Bhagavad Gita 10.37 — I am Vasudeva among the descendants of Vrishni, and Arjuna among the Pandavas. Among sages also, I am Vyasa; and among the discerning ones, I am the discerning Usanas.
Bhagavad Gita 10.38 — I am the rod of those that restrain, and the policy of those that desire victory. I am silence respecting secrets. I am the knowledge of those that have knowledge.
Bhagavad Gita 10.39 — And, O Arjuna! I am also that which is the seed of all things. There is nothing movable or immovable which can exist without me.
Bhagavad Gita 10.40 — O terror of your foes! there is no end to my divine emanations. Here I have declared the extent of (those) emanations only in part.
Bhagavad Gita 10.41 — Whatever thing (there is) of power, or glorious, or splendid, know all that to be produced from portions of my energy.
Bhagavad Gita 10.42 — Or rather, O Arjuna! what have you to do, knowing all this at large? I stand supporting all this by (but) a single portion (of myself).

Bhagavad Gita 11.1 — Arjuna said: In consequence of the excellent and mysterious words concerning the relation of the supreme and individual soul, which you have spoken for my welfare, this delusion of mine is gone away.
Bhagavad Gita 11.2 — O you whose eyes are like lotus leaves! I have heard from you at large about the production and dissolution of things, and also about your inexhaustible greatness.
Bhagavad Gita 11.3 — O highest lord! what you have said about yourself is so. I wish, O best of beings! to see your divine form.
Bhagavad Gita 11.4 — If, O lord! you think that it is possible for me to look upon it, then, O lord of the possessors of mystic power! show your inexhaustible form to me.
Bhagavad Gita 11.5 — The Deity said: In hundreds and in thousands see my forms, O son of Pritha! various, divine, and of various colours and shapes.
Bhagavad Gita 11.6 — See the Adityas, Vasus, Rudras, the two Asvins, and Maruts likewise. And O descendant of Bharata! see wonders, in numbers, unseen before.
Bhagavad Gita 11.7 — Within my body, O Gudakesa! see to-day the whole universe, including (everything) movable and immovable, (all) in one, and whatever else you wish to see.
Bhagavad Gita 11.8 — But you will not be able to see me with merely this eye of yours. I give you an eye divine. (Now) see my divine power.
Bhagavad Gita 11.9 — Sanjaya said: Having spoken thus, O king! Hari, the great lord of the possessors of mystic power, then showed to the son of Pritha his supreme divine form.
Bhagavad Gita 11.10 — Having many mouths and eyes, having (within it) many wonderful sights, having many celestial ornaments, having many celestial weapons held erect.
Bhagavad Gita 11.11 — Wearing celestial flowers and vestments, having an anointment of celestial perfumes, full of every wonder, the infinite deity with faces in all directions.
Bhagavad Gita 11.12 — If in the heavens, the lustre of a thousand suns burst forth all at once, that would be like the lustre of that mighty one.
Bhagavad Gita 11.13 — There the son of Pandu then observed in the body of the god of gods the whole universe (all) in one, and divided into numerous (divisions).
Bhagavad Gita 11.14 — Then Dhananjaya filled with amazement, and with hair standing on end, bowed his head before the god, and spoke with joined hands.

Bhagavad Gita 11.15 — Arjuna said: O god! I see within your body the gods, as also all the groups of various beings; and the lord Brahman seated on (his) lotus seat, and all the sages and celestial snakes.

Bhagavad Gita 11.16 — I see you, who are of countless forms, possessed of many arms, stomachs, mouths, and eyes on all sides. And, O lord of the universe! O you of all forms! I do not see your end or middle or beginning.

Bhagavad Gita 11.17 — I see you bearing a coronet and a mace and a discus—a mass of glory, brilliant on all sides, difficult to look at, having on all sides the effulgence of a blazing fire or sun, and indefinable.

Bhagavad Gita 11.18 — You are indestructible, the supreme one to be known. You are the highest support of this universe. You are the inexhaustible protector of everlasting piety. I believe you to be the eternal being.

Bhagavad Gita 11.19 — I see you void of beginning, middle, end—of infinite power, of unnumbered arms, having the sun and moon for eyes, having a mouth like a blazing fire, and heating the universe with your radiance.

Bhagavad Gita 11.20 — For this space between heaven and earth and all the quarters are pervaded by you alone. Looking at this wonderful and terrible form of yours, O high-souled one! the three worlds are affrighted.

Bhagavad Gita 11.21 — For here these groups of gods are entering into you. Some being afraid are praying with joined hands, and the groups of great sages and Siddhas are saying 'Welfare!' and praising you with abundant (hymns) of praise.

Bhagavad Gita 11.22 — The Rudras, and Adityas, the Vasus, the Sadhyas, the Visvas, the two Asvins, the Maruts, and the Ushmapas, and the groups of Gandharvas, Yakshas, demons, and Siddhas are all looking at you amazed.

Bhagavad Gita 11.23 — Seeing your mighty form, with many mouths and eyes, with many arms, thighs, and feet, with many stomachs, and fearful with many jaws, all people, and I likewise, are much alarmed, O you of mighty arms!

Bhagavad Gita 11.24 — Seeing you, O Vishnu! touching the skies, radiant, possessed of many hues, with a gaping mouth, and with large blazing eyes, I am much alarmed in my inmost self, and feel no courage, no tranquillity.
