Bhagavad Gita 11.25 — And seeing your mouths terrible by the jaws, and resembling the fire of destruction, I cannot recognise the (various) directions, I feel no comfort. Be gracious, O lord of gods! who pervadest the universe.
Bhagavad Gita 11.26 — And all these sons of Dhritarashtra, together with all the bands of kings, and Bhishma and Drona, and this charioteer's son likewise, together with our principal warriors also.
Bhagavad Gita 11.27 — Are rapidly entering your mouths, fearful and horrific by (reason of your) jaws. And some with their heads smashed are seen (to be) stuck in the spaces between the teeth.
Bhagavad Gita 11.28 — As the many rapid currents of a river's waters run towards the sea alone, so do these heroes of the human world enter your mouths blazing all round.
Bhagavad Gita 11.29 — As butterflies, with increased velocity, enter a blazing fire to their destruction, so too do these people enter your mouths with increased velocity (only) to their destruction.

Bhagavad Gita 11.30 — Swallowing all these people, you are licking them over and over again from all sides, with your blazing mouths. Your fierce splendours, O Vishnu! filling the whole universe with (their) effulgence, are heating it.
Bhagavad Gita 11.31 — Tell me who you are in this fierce form. Salutations be to thee, O chief of the gods! Be gracious. I wish to know you, the primeval one, for I do not understand your actions.

Bhagavad Gita 11.32 — The Deity said: I am death, the destroyer of the worlds, fully developed, and I am now active about the overthrow of the worlds. Even without you, the warriors standing in the adverse hosts, shall all cease to be.
Bhagavad Gita 11.33 — Therefore, be up, obtain glory, and vanquishing (your) foes, enjoy a prosperous kingdom. All these have been already killed by me. Be only the instrument, O Savyasachin!

Bhagavad Gita 11.34 — Drona, and Bhishma, and Jayadratha, and Karna, and likewise other valiant warriors also, whom I have killed, do you kill. Be not alarmed. Do fight. And in the battle you will conquer your foes.

Bhagavad Gita 11.35 — Sanjaya said: Hearing these words of Kesava, the wearer of the coronet, trembling, and with joined hands, bowed down; and sorely afraid, and with throat choked up, he again spoke to Krishna after saluting him.

Bhagavad Gita 11.36 — Arjuna said: It is quite proper, O Hrishikesa! that the universe is delighted and charmed by your renown, that the demons run away affrighted in all directions, and that all the assemblages of Siddhas bow down (to you).

Bhagavad Gita 11.37 — And why, O high-souled one! should they not bow down to you (who are) greater than Brahman, and first cause? O infinite lord of gods! O you pervading the universe! you are the indestructible, that which is, that which is not, and what is beyond them.

Bhagavad Gita 11.38 — You are the primal god, the ancient being, you are the highest support of this universe. You are that which has knowledge, that which is the object of knowledge, you are the highest goal. By you is this universe pervaded, O you of infinite forms!
Bhagavad Gita 11.39 — You are the wind, Yama, fire, Varuna, the moon, you Prajapati, and the great grandsire. Obeisance be to thee a thousand times, and again and again obeisance to thee!

Bhagavad Gita 11.40 — In front and from behind obeisance to thee! Obeisance be to thee from all sides, O you who are all! You are of infinite power, of unmeasured glory; you pervade all, and therefore you are all!

Bhagavad Gita 11.41 — Whatever I have said contemptuously,—for instance, 'O Krishna!' 'O Yadava!' 'O friend!'—thinking you to be (my) friend, and not knowing your greatness (as shown in) this (universal form), or through friendliness, or incautiously.

Bhagavad Gita 11.42 — And whatever disrespect I have shown you for purposes of merriment, on (occasions of) play, sleep, dinner, or sitting (together), whether alone or in the presence (of friends),—for all that, O undegraded one! I ask pardon of you who are indefinable.

Bhagavad Gita 11.43 — You are the father of the world—movable and immovable,—you its great and venerable master; there is none equal to you, whence can there be one greater, O you whose power is unparalleled in all the three worlds?

Bhagavad Gita 11.44 — Therefore I bow and prostrate myself, and would propitiate you, the praiseworthy lord. Be pleased, O god! to pardon (my guilt) as a father (that of his) son, a friend (that of his) friend, or a husband (that of his) beloved.

Bhagavad Gita 11.45 — I am delighted at seeing what I had never seen before, and my heart is also alarmed by fear. Show me that same form, O god! Be gracious, O lord of gods! O you pervading the universe!

Bhagavad Gita 11.46 — I wish to see you bearing the coronet and the mace, with the discus in hand, just the same (as before). O you of thousand arms! O you of all forms! assume that same four-handed form.

Bhagavad Gita 11.47 — The Deity said: O Arjuna! being pleased (with you), I have by my own mystic power shown you this supreme form, full of glory, universal, infinite, primeval, and which has not been seen before by any one else but you, O you hero among the Kauravas!
Bhagavad Gita 11.48 — I cannot be seen in this form by any one but you, (even) by (the help of) the study of the Vedas, or of sacrifices, nor by gifts, nor by actions, nor by fierce penances.
Bhagavad Gita 11.49 — Be not alarmed, be not perplexed, at seeing this form of mine, fearful like this. Free from fear and with delighted heart, see now again that same form of mine.
Bhagavad Gita 11.50 — Sanjaya said: Having thus spoken to Arjuna, Vasudeva again showed his own form, and the high-souled one becoming again of a mild form, comforted him who had been affrighted.
Bhagavad Gita 11.51 — Arjuna said: O Janardana! seeing this mild, human form of yours, I am now in my right mind, and have come to my normal state.
Bhagavad Gita 11.52 — The Deity said: Even the gods are always desiring to see this form of mine, which it is difficult to get a sight of, and which you have seen.
Bhagavad Gita 11.53 — I cannot be seen, as you have seen me, by (means of) the Vedas, not by penance, not by gift, nor yet by sacrifice.
Bhagavad Gita 11.54 — But, O Arjuna! by devotion to me exclusively, I can in this form be truly known, seen, and assimilated with, O terror of your foes!

Bhagavad Gita 11.55 — He who performs acts for (propitiating) me, to whom I am the highest (object), who is my devotee, who is free from attachment, and who has no enmity towards any being, he, O son of Pandu! comes to me.
Bhagavad Gita 12.1 — Arjuna said: Of the worshippers, who thus, constantly devoted, meditate on you, and those who (meditate) on the unperceived and indestructible, which best know devotion?
Bhagavad Gita 12.2 — The Deity said: Those who being constantly devoted, and possessed of the highest faith, worship me with a mind fixed on me, are deemed by me to be the most devoted.

Bhagavad Gita 12.3 — But those, who, restraining the (whole) group of the senses, and with a mind at all times equable, meditate on the indescribable, indestructible, unperceived (principle) which is all-pervading, unthinkable, indifferent, immovable, and constant, they, intent on the good of all beings, necessarily attain to me.

Bhagavad Gita 12.4 — But those, who, restraining the (whole) group of the senses, and with a mind at all times equable, meditate on the indescribable, indestructible, unperceived (principle) which is all-pervading, unthinkable, indifferent, immovable, and constant, they, intent on the good of all beings, necessarily attain to me.
Bhagavad Gita 12.5 — For those whose minds are attached to the unperceived, the trouble is much greater. Because the unperceived goal is obtained by embodied (beings) with difficulty.

Bhagavad Gita 12.6 — As to those, however, O son of Pritha! who, dedicating all their actions to me, and (holding) me as their highest (goal), worship me, meditating on me with a devotion towards none besides me.
Bhagavad Gita 12.7 — And whose minds are fixed on me, I, without delay, come forward as their deliverer from the ocean of this world of death.
Bhagavad Gita 12.8 — Place your mind on me only; fix your understanding on me. In me you will dwell hereafter, (there is) no doubt.
Bhagavad Gita 12.9 — But if you are unable to fix your mind steadily on me, then, O Dhananjaya! endeavour to obtain me by the abstraction of mind (resulting) from continuous meditation.

Bhagavad Gita 12.10 — If you are unequal even to continuous meditation, then let acts for (propitiating) me be your highest (aim). Even performing actions for (propitiating) me, you will attain perfection.
Bhagavad Gita 12.11 — If you are unable to do even this, then resort to devotion to me, and, with self-restraint, abandon all fruit of action.

Bhagavad Gita 12.12 — For knowledge is better than continuous meditation; concentration is esteemed higher than knowledge; and the abandonment of fruit of action than concentration; from (that) abandonment, tranquillity soon (results).

Bhagavad Gita 12.13 — That devotee of mine, who hates no being, who is friendly and compassionate, who is free from egoism, and from (the idea that this or that is) mine, to whom happiness and misery are alike, who is forgiving…
Bhagavad Gita 12.14 — [Who is] contented, constantly devoted, self-restrained, and firm in his determinations, and whose mind and understanding are devoted to me, he is dear to me.
Bhagavad Gita 12.15 — He through whom the world is not agitated, and who is not agitated by the world, who is free from joy and anger and fear and agitation, he too is dear to me.
Bhagavad Gita 12.16 — That devotee of mine, who is unconcerned, pure, assiduous, impartial, free from distress, who abandons all actions (for fruit), he is dear to me.

Bhagavad Gita 12.17 — He who is full of devotion to me, who feels no joy and no aversion, who does not grieve and does not desire, who abandons (both what is) agreeable and (what is) disagreeable, he is dear to me.
Bhagavad Gita 12.18 — He who is alike to friend and foe, as also in honour and dishonour, who is alike in cold and heat, pleasure and pain, who is free from attachments…

Bhagavad Gita 12.19 — [He] to whom praise and blame are alike, who is taciturn, and contented with anything whatever (that comes), who is homeless, and of a steady mind, and full of devotion, that man is dear to me.

Bhagavad Gita 12.20 — But those devotees who, imbued with faith, and (regarding) me as their highest (goal), resort to this holy (means for attaining) immortality, as stated, they are extremely dear to me.
Bhagavad Gita 13.1 — Arjuna said: O Kesava, I would learn of nature and spirit, of the field and the one who knows the field, and of knowledge and what is to be known.
Bhagavad Gita 13.2 — The Deity said: This body, O son of Kunti! is called Kshetra, and the learned call him who knows it the Kshetrajna.
Bhagavad Gita 13.3 — And know me also, O descendant of Bharata! to be the Kshetrajna in all Kshetras. The knowledge of Kshetra and Kshetrajna is deemed by me (to be real) knowledge.
Bhagavad Gita 13.4 — Now hear from me in brief what that Kshetra (is), what (it is) like, what changes (it undergoes), and whence (it comes), and what is he, and what his powers.
Bhagavad Gita 13.5 — (all which) is sung in various ways by sages in numerous hymns, distinctly, and in well-settled texts full of argument, giving indications or full instruction about the Brahman.
Bhagavad Gita 13.6 — The great elements, egoism, the understanding, the unperceived also, the ten senses, and the one, and the five objects of sense.
Bhagavad Gita 13.7 — Desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, body, consciousness, courage, thus in brief has been declared the Kshetra with changes.
Bhagavad Gita 13.8 — Absence of vanity, absence of ostentatiousness, absence of hurtfulness, forgiveness, straightforwardness, devotion to a preceptor, purity, steadiness, self-restraint.
Bhagavad Gita 13.9 — Indifference towards objects of sense, and also absence of egoism; perception of the misery and evil of birth, death, old age, and disease.

Bhagavad Gita 13.10 — Absence of attachment, absence of self-identifying regard for son, wife, home, and so forth; and constant equability on the approach of (both what is) agreeable and (what is) disagreeable.
Bhagavad Gita 13.11 — Unswerving devotion to me, without meditation on any one else; resorting to clean places, distaste for assemblages of men.

Bhagavad Gita 13.12 — Constancy in knowledge of the relation of the individual self to the supreme, perception of the object of knowledge of the truth, this is called knowledge; that is ignorance which is opposed to this.

Bhagavad Gita 13.13 — I will declare that which is the object of knowledge, knowing which, one reaches immortality; the highest Brahman, having no beginning nor end, which cannot be said to be existent or non-existent.
Bhagavad Gita 13.14 — It has hands and feet on all sides, it has eyes, heads, and faces on all sides, it has ears on all sides, it stands pervading everything in the world.
Bhagavad Gita 13.15 — Possessed of the qualities of all the senses, (but) devoid of all senses, unattached, it supports all, is devoid of qualities, and the enjoyer of qualities.
Bhagavad Gita 13.16 — It is within all things and without them; it is movable and also immovable; it is unknowable through (its) subtlety; it stands afar and near.
Bhagavad Gita 13.17 — Not different in (different) things, but standing as though different, it should be known to be the supporter of (all) things, and that which absorbs and creates (them).

Bhagavad Gita 13.18 — It is the radiance even of the radiant (bodies); it is said (to be) beyond darkness. It is knowledge, the object of knowledge, that which is to be attained to by knowledge, and placed in the heart of all.
Bhagavad Gita 13.19 — Thus in brief have Kshetra, knowledge, and the object of knowledge been declared. My devotee, knowing this, becomes fit for assimilation with me.
Bhagavad Gita 13.20 — Know nature and spirit both (to be) without beginning, and know all developments and qualities (to be) produced from nature.

Bhagavad Gita 13.21 — Nature is said to be the origin of the capacity of working (residing) in the body and the senses; and spirit is said (to be) the origin of the capacity of enjoying pleasures and pains.
Bhagavad Gita 13.22 — For spirit with nature joined, enjoys the qualities born of nature. And the cause of its birth in good or evil wombs is the connexion with the qualities.
Bhagavad Gita 13.23 — The supreme spirit in this body is called supervisor, adviser, supporter, enjoyer, the great lord, and the supreme self also.
Bhagavad Gita 13.24 — He who thus knows nature and spirit, together with the qualities, is not born again, however living.
Bhagavad Gita 13.25 — Some by concentration see the self in the self by the self; others by the Sankhya-yoga; and others still by the Karma-yoga.
Bhagavad Gita 13.26 — Others yet, not knowing this, practise concentration, after hearing from others. They, too, being (thus) devoted to hearing (instruction) cross beyond death.
Bhagavad Gita 13.27 — Whatever thing movable or immovable comes into existence, know that to be from the connexion of Kshetra and Kshetrajna, O chief of the descendants of Bharata!
Bhagavad Gita 13.28 — He sees (truly) who sees the supreme lord abiding alike in all entities, and not destroyed though they are destroyed.
Bhagavad Gita 13.29 — For he who sees the lord abiding everywhere alike, does not destroy himself by himself, and then reaches the highest goal.
Bhagavad Gita 13.30 — He sees (truly), who sees (all) actions (to be) in every way done by nature alone, and likewise the self (to be) not the doer.
Bhagavad Gita 13.31 — When a man sees all the variety of entities as existing in one, and (all as) emanating from that, then he becomes (one with) the Brahman.
Bhagavad Gita 13.32 — This inexhaustible supreme self, being without beginning and without qualities, does not act, and is not tainted, O son of Kunti! though stationed in the body.
Bhagavad Gita 13.33 — As by (reason of its) subtlety the all-pervading space is not tainted, so the self stationed in every body is not tainted.
Bhagavad Gita 13.34 — As the sun singly lights up all this world, so the Kshetrajna, O descendant of Bharata! lights up the whole Kshetra.
Bhagavad Gita 13.35 — Those who, with the eye of knowledge, thus understand the difference between Kshetra and Kshetrajna, and the destruction of the nature of all entities, go to the supreme.

Bhagavad Gita 14.1 — The Deity said: Again I will declare (to you) the highest knowledge, the best of (all sorts of) knowledge, having learnt which, all sages have reached perfection beyond (the bonds of) this (body).
Bhagavad Gita 14.2 — Those who, resorting to this knowledge, reach assimilation with my essence, are not born at the creation, and are not afflicted at the destruction (of the universe).
Bhagavad Gita 14.3 — The great Brahman is a womb for me, in which I cast the seed. From that, O descendant of Bharata! is the birth of all things.
Bhagavad Gita 14.4 — Of the bodies, O son of Kunti! which are born from all wombs, the (main) womb is the great Brahman, and I (am) the father, the giver of the seed.
Bhagavad Gita 14.5 — Goodness, passion, darkness, these qualities born from nature, O you of mighty arms! bind down the inexhaustible soul in the body.

Bhagavad Gita 14.6 — Of these, goodness, which, in consequence of being untainted, is enlightening and free from (all) misery, binds the soul, O sinless one! with the bond of pleasure and the bond of knowledge.
Bhagavad Gita 14.7 — Know that passion consists in being enamoured, and is produced from craving and attachment. That, O son of Kunti! binds down the embodied (self) with the bond of action.

Bhagavad Gita 14.8 — Darkness (you must) know to be born of ignorance, it deludes all embodied (selfs). And that, O descendant of Bharata! binds down (the self) with heedlessness, indolence, and sleep.
Bhagavad Gita 14.9 — Goodness unites (the self) with pleasure; passion, O descendant of Bharata! with action; and darkness with heedlessness, after shrouding up knowledge.

Bhagavad Gita 14.10 — Passion and darkness being repressed, goodness stands, O descendant of Bharata! Passion and goodness (being repressed), darkness; and likewise darkness and goodness (being repressed), passion.
Bhagavad Gita 14.11 — When in this body at all portals light (that is to say) knowledge prevails, then should one know goodness to be developed.
Bhagavad Gita 14.12 — Avarice, activity, performance of actions, want of tranquillity, desire, these are produced, O chief of the descendants of Bharata! when passion is developed.
Bhagavad Gita 14.13 — Want of light, want of activity, heedlessness, and delusion, these are produced, O descendant of Kuru! when darkness is developed.
Bhagavad Gita 14.14 — When an embodied (self) encounters death, while goodness is developed, then he reaches the untainted worlds of those who know the highest.

Bhagavad Gita 14.15 — Encountering death during (the prevalence of) passion, he is born among those attached to action. Likewise, dying during (the prevalence of) darkness, he is born in the wombs of the ignorant.
Bhagavad Gita 14.16 — The fruit of meritorious action is said to be good, untainted; while the fruit of passion is misery; and the fruit of darkness ignorance.
Bhagavad Gita 14.17 — From goodness is produced knowledge, from passion avarice, and from darkness heedlessness and delusion and ignorance also.

Bhagavad Gita 14.18 — Those who adhere to (the ways of) goodness go up; the passionate remain in the middle; while those of the qualities of darkness, adhering to the ways of the lowest quality, go down.
Bhagavad Gita 14.19 — When a right-seeing person sees none but the qualities (to be) the doers (of all action), and knows what is above the qualities, he enters into my essence.
Bhagavad Gita 14.20 — The embodied (self), who transcends these three qualities, from which bodies are produced, attains immortality, being freed from birth and death and old age and misery.
Bhagavad Gita 14.21 — Arjuna said: What are the characteristics, O lord! of one who has transcended these three qualities? What is his conduct, and how does he transcend these three qualities?

Bhagavad Gita 14.22 — The Deity said: He is said to have transcended the qualities, O son of Pandu! who is not averse to light and activity and delusion (when they) prevail, and who does not desire (them when they) cease.
Bhagavad Gita 14.23 — Who sitting like one unconcerned is never perturbed by the qualities; who remains steady and moves not, (thinking) merely that the qualities exist.

Bhagavad Gita 14.24 — Who is self-contained; to whom pain and pleasure are alike; to whom a sod and a stone and gold are alike; to whom what is agreeable and what is disagreeable are alike; who has discernment; to whom censure and praise of himself are alike.
Bhagavad Gita 14.25 — Who is alike in honour and dishonour; who is alike towards the sides of friends and foes; and who abandons all action.
Bhagavad Gita 14.26 — And he who worships me with an unswerving devotion, transcends these qualities, and becomes fit for (entrance into) the essence of the Brahman.
Bhagavad Gita 14.27 — For I am the embodiment of the Brahman, of indefeasible immortality, of eternal piety, and of unbroken happiness.
Bhagavad Gita 15.1 — The Deity said: They say the inexhaustible Asvattha has (its) roots above, (its) branches below; the Khandas are its leaves. He who knows it knows the Vedas.

Bhagavad Gita 15.2 — Upwards and downwards extend its branches, which are enlarged by the qualities, and the sprouts of which are sensuous objects. And downwards to this human world are continued its roots which lead on to action.
Bhagavad Gita 15.3 — Its form is not thus known here, nor (its) end, nor beginning, nor support. But having with the firm weapon of unconcern, cut this Asvattha, whose roots are firmly fixed.

Bhagavad Gita 15.4 — Then should one seek for that seat from which those that go there never return, (thinking) that one rests on that same primal being from whom the ancient course (of worldly life) emanated.

Bhagavad Gita 15.5 — Those who are free from pride and delusion, who have overcome the evils of attachment, who are constant in (contemplating) the relation of the supreme and individual self, from whom desire has departed, who are free from the pairs (of opposites) called pleasure and pain, go undeluded to that imperishable seat.
Bhagavad Gita 15.6 — The sun does not light it, nor the moon, nor fire. That is my highest abode, going to which none returns.
Bhagavad Gita 15.7 — An eternal portion of me it is, which, becoming an individual soul in the mortal world, draws (to itself) the senses with the mind as the sixth.
Bhagavad Gita 15.8 — Whenever the ruler (of the bodily frame) obtains or quits a body, he goes taking these (with him) as the wind (takes) perfumes from (their) seats.
Bhagavad Gita 15.9 — And presiding over the senses of hearing and seeing, and touch, and taste, and smell, and the mind, he enjoys sensuous objects.
Bhagavad Gita 15.10 — Those who are deluded do not see (him) remaining in or quitting (a body), enjoying or joined to the qualities; they see, who have eyes of knowledge.

Bhagavad Gita 15.11 — Devotees making efforts perceive him abiding within their selfs. But those whose selfs have not been refined, and who have no discernment, do not perceive him even (after) making efforts.
Bhagavad Gita 15.12 — Know that glory (to be) mine which, dwelling in the sun, lights up the whole world, or in the moon or fire.
Bhagavad Gita 15.13 — Entering the earth, I by my power support all things; and becoming the juicy moon, I nourish all herbs.
Bhagavad Gita 15.14 — I becoming the fire, and dwelling in the bodies of (all) creatures, and united with the upward and downward life-breaths, cause digestion of the fourfold food.

Bhagavad Gita 15.15 — And I am placed in the heart of all; from me (come) memory, knowledge, and their removal; I alone am to be learnt from all the Vedas; I am the author of the Vedantas; and I alone know the Vedas.

Bhagavad Gita 15.16 — There are these two beings in the world, the destructible and the indestructible. The destructible (includes) all things. The unconcerned one is (what is) called the indestructible.
Bhagavad Gita 15.17 — But the being supreme is yet another, called the highest self, who as the inexhaustible lord, pervading the three worlds, supports (them).
Bhagavad Gita 15.18 — And since I transcend the destructible, and since I am higher also than the indestructible, therefore am I celebrated in the world and in the Vedas as the best of beings.
Bhagavad Gita 15.19 — He who, undeluded, thus knows me the best of beings, worships me every way, O descendant of Bharata! knowing everything.
Bhagavad Gita 15.20 — Thus, O sinless one! have I proclaimed this most mysterious science. He who knows this, has done all he need do, and he becomes possessed of discernment.

Bhagavad Gita 16.1 — Freedom from fear, purity of heart, perseverance in (pursuit of) knowledge and abstraction of mind, gifts, self-restraint, and sacrifice, study of the Vedas, penance, straightforwardness.

Bhagavad Gita 16.2 — Harmlessness, truth, freedom from anger, renunciation, tranquillity, freedom from the habit of backbiting, compassion for (all) beings, freedom from avarice, gentleness, modesty, absence of vain activity.

Bhagavad Gita 16.3 — Noblemindedness, forgiveness, courage, purity, freedom from a desire to injure others, absence of vanity, (these), O descendant of Bharata! are his who is born to godlike endowments.
Bhagavad Gita 16.4 — Ostentatiousness, pride, vanity, anger, and also harshness and ignorance (are) his, O son of Pritha! who is born to demoniac endowments.
Bhagavad Gita 16.5 — Godlike endowments are deemed to be (means) for final emancipation, demoniac for bondage. Grieve not, O descendant of Bharata! you are born to godlike endowments.

Bhagavad Gita 16.6 — (There are) two classes of created beings in this world, the godlike and the demoniac; the godlike (class) has been described at length; now hear from me, O son of Pritha! about the demoniac.
Bhagavad Gita 16.7 — Demoniac persons know not action or inaction, neither purity nor yet (correct) conduct nor veracity are in them.
Bhagavad Gita 16.8 — They say the universe is devoid of truth, devoid of fixed principle, and devoid of a ruler, produced by union (of male and female) caused by lust, and nothing else.
Bhagavad Gita 16.9 — Holding this view, (these) enemies of the world, of ruined selfs, of little knowledge, and of ferocious actions, are born for the destruction (of the world).
Bhagavad Gita 16.10 — Entertaining insatiable desire, full of vanity, ostentatiousness, and frenzy, they adopt false notions through delusion, and engage in unholy observances.
Bhagavad Gita 16.11 — Indulging in boundless thoughts ending with death, given up to the enjoyment of objects of desire, being resolved that that is all.
Bhagavad Gita 16.12 — Bound down by nets of hopes in hundreds, given up to anger and desire, they wish to obtain heaps of wealth unfairly for enjoying objects of desire.
Bhagavad Gita 16.13 — This have I obtained to-day; this wish I will obtain; this wealth is mine; and this also shall be mine.
Bhagavad Gita 16.14 — This foe I have killed; others too I will destroy; I am lord, I am the enjoyer, I am perfect, strong, happy.
Bhagavad Gita 16.15 — I have wealth; I am of noble birth; who else is like me? I will sacrifice; I will make gifts; I will rejoice. Thus deluded by ignorance.
Bhagavad Gita 16.16 — Tossed about by numerous thoughts, surrounded by the net of delusion, and attached to the enjoyment of objects of desire, they fall down into impure hell.

Bhagavad Gita 16.17 — Honoured (only) by themselves, void of humility, and full of the pride and frenzy of wealth, these calumniators (of the virtuous) perform sacrifices, which are sacrifices only in name, with ostentatiousness and against prescribed rules.
Bhagavad Gita 16.18 — Indulging (their) vanity, brute force, arrogance, lust, and anger; and hating me in their own bodies and in those of others.
Bhagavad Gita 16.19 — These enemies, ferocious, meanest of men, and unholy, I continually hurl down, to these worlds, only into demoniac wombs.
Bhagavad Gita 16.20 — Coming into demoniac wombs, deluded in every birth, they go down to the vilest state, O son of Kunti! without ever coming to me.
Bhagavad Gita 16.21 — Threefold is this way, to hell,—ruinous to the self,—lust, anger, and likewise avarice; therefore one should abandon this triad.
Bhagavad Gita 16.22 — Released from these three ways to darkness, O son of Kunti! a man works out his own welfare, and then proceeds to the highest goal.
Bhagavad Gita 16.23 — He who abandoning scripture ordinances, acts under the impulse of desire, does not attain perfection, nor happiness, nor the highest goal.

Bhagavad Gita 16.24 — Therefore in discriminating between what should be done and what should not be done, your authority (must be) scripture. And knowing what is declared by the ordinances of scripture, you should perform action in this world.
Bhagavad Gita 17.1 — Arjuna said: What is the state of those, O Krishna! who worship with faith, (but) abandoning scripture ordinances—goodness, passion, or darkness?

Bhagavad Gita 17.2 — The Deity said: Faith is of three kinds in embodied (beings), it is produced from dispositions. It is of the quality of goodness, of the quality of passion, and of the quality of darkness. Hear about it.
Bhagavad Gita 17.3 — The faith of all, O descendant of Bharata! is conformable to the heart. A being here is full of faith, and whatever is a man's faith, that is a man himself.

Bhagavad Gita 17.4 — Those of the quality of goodness worship the gods; those of the quality of passion the Yakshas and Rakshasas; and the others, the people of the quality of darkness, worship departed (spirits) and the multitudes of Bhutas.

Bhagavad Gita 17.5 — Know those to be of demoniac convictions, who practise fierce penance not ordained by scripture; who are full of ostentatiousness and egoism, and of desire, attachment, and stubbornness; who are without discernment.
Bhagavad Gita 17.6 — And who torment the groups of organs in (their) bodies, and me also seated within (those) bodies.
Bhagavad Gita 17.7 — The food also, which is liked by all, and likewise the sacrifice, the penance, and gifts, are of three kinds. Listen to the distinctions regarding them as follows.
Bhagavad Gita 17.8 — The kinds of food which increase life, energy, strength, health, comfort, and relish, which are savoury, oleaginous, full of nutrition, and agreeable, are liked by the good.
Bhagavad Gita 17.9 — The kinds of food which are bitter, acid, saltish, too hot, sharp, rough, and burning, and which cause pain, grief, and disease, are desired by the passionate.
Bhagavad Gita 17.10 — And the food which is cold, tasteless, stinking, stale, impure, and even leavings, are liked by the dark.

Bhagavad Gita 17.11 — That sacrifice is good which, being prescribed in (scripture) ordinances, is performed by persons not wishing for the fruit (of it), and after determining (in their) mind that the sacrifice must needs be performed.

Bhagavad Gita 17.12 — But when a sacrifice is performed, O highest of the descendants of Bharata! with an expectation of fruit (from it), and for the purpose of ostentation, know that sacrifice (to be) passionate.

Bhagavad Gita 17.13 — They call that sacrifice dark, which is against the ordinances (of scripture), in which no food is dealt out (to Brahmanas, &c.), which is devoid of Mantras, devoid of Dakshina presents, and which is without faith.
Bhagavad Gita 17.14 — Paying reverence to gods, Brahmanas, preceptors, and men of knowledge; purity, straightforwardness, life as Brahmacharin, and harmlessness, (this) is called the penance bodily.
Bhagavad Gita 17.15 — The speech which causes no sorrow, which is true, agreeable, and beneficial, and the study of the Vedas, (this) is called the penance vocal.
Bhagavad Gita 17.16 — Calmness of mind, mildness, taciturnity, self-restraint, and purity of heart, this is called the penance mental.
Bhagavad Gita 17.17 — This threefold penance, practised with perfect faith, by men who do not wish for the fruit, and who are possessed of devotion is called good.
Bhagavad Gita 17.18 — The penance which is done for respect, honour, and reverence, and with ostentatiousness, and which is uncertain and transient, is here called passionate.
Bhagavad Gita 17.19 — And that penance is described as dark, which is performed under a misguided conviction, with pain to oneself, or for the destruction of another.
Bhagavad Gita 17.20 — That gift is said (to be) good, which is given, because it ought to be given, to one who (can) do no service (in return), at a (proper) place and time, and to a (proper) person.
Bhagavad Gita 17.21 — But that gift which is given with much difficulty, for a return of services, or even with an expectation of fruit, is said to be passionate.
Bhagavad Gita 17.22 — And that gift, is described as dark, which is given to unfit persons, at an unfit place and time, without respect, and with contempt.
Bhagavad Gita 17.23 — Om, Tad, and Sat, this is said (to be) the threefold designation of the Brahman. By that, the Brahmanas and the Vedas and sacrifices were created in olden times.
Bhagavad Gita 17.24 — Hence, the performance by those who study the Brahman, of sacrifices, gifts, and penances, prescribed by the ordinances (of scripture), always commence after saying 'Om.'
Bhagavad Gita 17.25 — Those who desire final emancipation perform the various acts of sacrifice and penance, and the various acts of gift, without expectation of fruit, after (saying) 'Tad.'
Bhagavad Gita 17.26 — 'Sat' is employed to express existence and goodness; and likewise, O son of Pritha! the word 'Sat' is used to express an auspicious act.
Bhagavad Gita 17.27 — Constancy in (making) sacrifices, penances, and gifts, is called 'Sat;' and (all) action, too, of which that is the object, is also called 'Sat.'

Bhagavad Gita 17.28 — Whatever oblation is offered, whatever is given, whatever penance is performed, and whatever is done, without faith, that, O son of Pritha! is called 'Asat,' and that is nought, both after death and here.
Bhagavad Gita 18.1 — Arjuna said: O you of mighty arms! O Hrishikesa! O destroyer of Kesin! I wish to know the truth about renunciation and abandonment distinctly.

Bhagavad Gita 18.2 — The Deity said: By renunciation the sages understand the rejection of actions done with desires. The wise call the abandonment of the fruit of all actions (by the name) abandonment.
Bhagavad Gita 18.3 — Some wise men say, that action should be abandoned as being full of evil; and others, that the actions of sacrifice, gift, and penance should not be abandoned.
Bhagavad Gita 18.4 — As to that abandonment, O best of the descendants of Bharata! listen to my decision; for abandonment, O bravest of men! is described (to be) threefold.
Bhagavad Gita 18.5 — The actions of sacrifice, gift, and penance should not be abandoned; they must needs be performed; for sacrifices, gifts, and penances are means of sanctification to the wise.
Bhagavad Gita 18.6 — But even these actions, O son of Pritha! should be performed, abandoning attachment and fruit; such is my excellent and decided opinion.
Bhagavad Gita 18.7 — The renunciation of prescribed action is not proper. Its abandonment through delusion is described as of the quality of darkness.
Bhagavad Gita 18.8 — When a man abandons action, merely as being troublesome, through fear of bodily affliction, he does not obtain the fruit of abandonment by making (such) passionate abandonment.
Bhagavad Gita 18.9 — When prescribed action is performed, O Arjuna! abandoning attachment and fruit also, merely because it ought to be performed, that is deemed (to be) a good abandonment.

Bhagavad Gita 18.10 — He who is possessed of abandonment, being full of goodness, and talented, and having his doubts destroyed, is not averse from unpleasant actions, is not attached to pleasant (ones).
Bhagavad Gita 18.11 — Since no embodied (being) can abandon actions without exception, he is said to be possessed of abandonment, who abandons the fruit of action.
Bhagavad Gita 18.12 — The threefold fruit of action, agreeable, disagreeable, and mixed, accrues after death to those who are not possessed of abandonment, but never to renouncers.
Bhagavad Gita 18.13 — Learn from me, O you of mighty arms! these five causes of the completion of all actions, declared in the Sankhya system.
Bhagavad Gita 18.14 — The substratum, the agent likewise, the various sorts of organs, and the various and distinct movements, and with these the deities, too, as the fifth.
Bhagavad Gita 18.15 — Whatever action, just or otherwise, a man performs with his body, speech, and mind, these five are its causes.
Bhagavad Gita 18.16 — That being so, the undiscerning man, who being of an unrefined understanding, sees the agent in the immaculate self, sees not (rightly).
Bhagavad Gita 18.17 — He who has no feeling of egoism, and whose mind is not tainted, even though he kills (all) these people, kills not, is not fettered (by the action).
Bhagavad Gita 18.18 — Knowledge, the object of knowledge, the knower—threefold is the prompting to action. The instrument, the action, the agent, thus in brief is action threefold.

Bhagavad Gita 18.19 — Knowledge and action and agent are declared in the enumeration of qualities (to be) of three classes only, according to the difference of qualities. Hear about these also as they really are.
Bhagavad Gita 18.20 — Know that knowledge to be good, by which (a man) sees one entity, inexhaustible, and not different in all things (apparently) different (from one another).
Bhagavad Gita 18.21 — Know that knowledge to be passionate, which is (based) on distinctions (between different entities), which sees in all things various entities of different kinds.
Bhagavad Gita 18.22 — And that is described as dark, which clings to one created (thing) only as everything, which is devoid of reason, devoid of real principle, and insignificant.

Bhagavad Gita 18.23 — That action is called good, which is prescribed, which is devoid of attachment, which is not done from (motives of) affection or aversion, (and which is done) by one not wishing for the fruit.
Bhagavad Gita 18.24 — That is described as passionate, which (occasions) much trouble, is performed by one who wishes for objects of desire, or one who is full of egotism.
Bhagavad Gita 18.25 — The action is called dark, which is commenced through delusion, without regard to consequences, loss, injury, or strength.
Bhagavad Gita 18.26 — That agent is called good, who has cast off attachment, who is free from egotistic talk, who is possessed of courage and energy, and unaffected by success or ill-success.
Bhagavad Gita 18.27 — That agent is called passionate, who is full of affections, who wishes for the fruit of actions, who is covetous, cruel, and impure, and feels joy and sorrow.
Bhagavad Gita 18.28 — That agent is called dark, who is without application, void of discernment, headstrong, crafty, malicious, lazy, melancholy, and slow.
Bhagavad Gita 18.29 — Now hear, O Dhananjaya! the threefold division of intelligence and courage, according to qualities, which I am about to declare exhaustively and distinctly.

Bhagavad Gita 18.30 — That intelligence, O son of Pritha! is good which understands action and inaction, what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, danger and the absence of danger, emancipation and bondage.
Bhagavad Gita 18.31 — That intelligence, O son of Pritha! is passionate, by which one imperfectly understands piety and impiety, what ought to be done and also what ought not to be done.
Bhagavad Gita 18.32 — That intelligence, O son of Pritha! is dark, which shrouded by darkness, understands impiety (to be) piety, and all things incorrectly.
Bhagavad Gita 18.33 — That courage, O son of Pritha! is good courage, which is unswerving, and by which one controls the operations of the mind, breath, and senses, through abstraction.
Bhagavad Gita 18.34 — But, O Arjuna! that courage is passionate, by which one adheres to piety, lust, and wealth, and through attachment wishes, O son of Pritha! for the fruit.
Bhagavad Gita 18.35 — That courage is dark, O son of Pritha! by which an undiscerning man does not give up sleep, fear, sorrow, despondency, and folly.

Bhagavad Gita 18.36 — Now, O chief of the descendants of Bharata! hear from me about the three sorts of happiness. That happiness is called good, in which one is pleased after repetition (of enjoyment), and reaches the close of all misery.
Bhagavad Gita 18.37 — Which is like poison first and comparable to nectar in the long run, and which is produced from a clear knowledge of the self.
Bhagavad Gita 18.38 — That happiness is called passionate, which (flows) from contact between the senses and their objects, and which is at first comparable to nectar and in the long run like poison.
Bhagavad Gita 18.39 — That happiness is described as dark, which arises from sleep, laziness, heedlessness, which deludes the self, both at first and in its consequences.
Bhagavad Gita 18.40 — There is no entity either on earth or in heaven among the gods, which is free from these three qualities born of nature.
Bhagavad Gita 18.41 — The duties of Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, and Vaisyas, and of Sudras, too, O terror of your foes! are distinguished according to the qualities born of nature.

Bhagavad Gita 18.42 — Tranquillity, restraint of the senses, penance, purity, forgiveness, straightforwardness, also knowledge, experience, and belief (in a future world), this is the natural duty of Brahmanas.
Bhagavad Gita 18.43 — Valour, glory, courage, dexterity, not slinking away from battle, gifts, exercise of lordly power, this is the natural duty of Kshatriyas.
Bhagavad Gita 18.44 — Agriculture, tending cattle, trade, (this) is the natural duty of Vaisyas. And the natural duty of Sudras, too, consists in service.
Bhagavad Gita 18.45 — (Every) man intent on his own respective duties obtains perfection. Listen, now, how one intent on one's own duty obtains perfection.
Bhagavad Gita 18.46 — Worshipping, by (the performance of) his own duty, him from whom all things proceed, and by whom all this is permeated, a man obtains perfection.
Bhagavad Gita 18.47 — One's duty, though defective, is better than another's duty well performed. Performing the duty prescribed by nature, one does not incur sin.
Bhagavad Gita 18.48 — O son of Kunti! one should not abandon a natural duty though tainted with evil; for all actions are enveloped by evil, as fire by smoke.

Bhagavad Gita 18.49 — One who is self-restrained, whose understanding is unattached everywhere, from whom affections have departed, obtains the supreme perfection of freedom from action by renunciation.
Bhagavad Gita 18.50 — Learn from me, only in brief, O son of Kunti! how one who has obtained perfection attains the Brahman, which is the highest culmination of knowledge.
Bhagavad Gita 18.51 — A man possessed of a pure understanding, controlling his self by courage, discarding sound and other objects of sense, casting off affection and aversion.

Bhagavad Gita 18.52 — Who frequents clean places, who eats little, whose speech, body, and mind are restrained, who is always intent on meditation and mental abstraction, and has recourse to unconcern.

Bhagavad Gita 18.53 — Who abandoning egoism, stubbornness, arrogance, desire, anger, and (all) belongings, has no (thought that this or that is) mine, and who is tranquil, becomes fit for assimilation with the Brahman.
Bhagavad Gita 18.54 — Thus reaching the Brahman, and with a tranquil self, he grieves not, wishes not; but being alike to all beings, obtains the highest devotion to me.
Bhagavad Gita 18.55 — By (that) devotion he truly understands who I am and how great. And then understanding me truly, he forthwith enters into my (essence).
Bhagavad Gita 18.56 — Even performing all actions, always depending on me, he, through my favour, obtains the imperishable and eternal seat.
Bhagavad Gita 18.57 — Dedicating in thought all actions to me, be constantly given up to me, (placing) your thoughts on me, through recourse to mental abstraction.
Bhagavad Gita 18.58 — (Placing) your thoughts on me, you will cross over all difficulties by my favour. But if you will not listen through egotism, you will be ruined.
Bhagavad Gita 18.59 — If entertaining egotism, you think that you may not fight, vain, indeed, is that resolution of yours. Nature will constrain you.
Bhagavad Gita 18.60 — That, O son of Kunti! which through delusion you do not wish to do, you will do involuntarily, tied down by your own duty, flowing from your nature.
Bhagavad Gita 18.61 — The lord, O Arjuna! is seated in the region of the heart of all beings, turning round all beings (as though) mounted on a machine, by his delusion.
Bhagavad Gita 18.62 — With him, O descendant of Bharata! seek shelter in every way; by his favour you will obtain the highest tranquillity, the eternal seat.
Bhagavad Gita 18.63 — Thus have I declared to you the knowledge more mysterious than any mystery. Ponder over it thoroughly, and then act as you like.
Bhagavad Gita 18.64 — Once more, listen to my excellent words—most mysterious of all. Strongly I like you, therefore I will declare what is for your welfare.
Bhagavad Gita 18.65 — On me (place) your mind, become my devotee, sacrifice to me, reverence me, you will certainly come to me. I declare to you truly, you are dear to me.
Bhagavad Gita 18.66 — Forsaking all duties, come to me as (your) sole refuge. I will release you from all sins. Be not grieved.
Bhagavad Gita 18.67 — This you should never declare to one who performs no penance, who is not a devotee, nor to one who does not wait on (some preceptor), nor yet to one who calumniates me.
Bhagavad Gita 18.68 — He who, with the highest devotion to me, will proclaim this supreme mystery among my devotees, will come to me, freed from (all) doubt.
Bhagavad Gita 18.69 — No one amongst men is superior to him in doing what is dear to me. And there will never be another on earth dearer to me than he.
Bhagavad Gita 18.70 — And he who will study this holy dialogue of ours, will, such is my opinion, have offered to me the sacrifice of knowledge.
Bhagavad Gita 18.71 — And the man, also, who with faith and without carping will listen (to this), will be freed (from sin), and attain to the holy regions of those who perform pious acts.
Bhagavad Gita 18.72 — Have you listened to this, O son of Pritha! with a mind (fixed) on (this) one point only? Has your delusion (caused) by ignorance been destroyed, O Dhananjaya?
Bhagavad Gita 18.73 — Arjuna said: Destroyed is my delusion; by your favour, O undegraded one! I (now) recollect myself. I stand freed from doubts. I will do your bidding.
Bhagavad Gita 18.74 — Sanjaya said: Thus did I hear this dialogue between Vasudeva and the high-minded son of Pritha, (a dialogue) wonderful and causing the hair to stand on end.
Bhagavad Gita 18.75 — By the favour of Vyasa, I heard this highest mystery, (this) devotion, from Krishna himself, the lord of the possessors of mystic power, who proclaimed it in person.
Bhagavad Gita 18.76 — O king! remembering and (again) remembering this wonderful and holy dialogue of Kesava and Arjuna, I rejoice over and over again.
Bhagavad Gita 18.77 — And remembering and (again) remembering that excessively wonderful form of Hari also, great is my amazement, O king! and I rejoice over and over again.

Bhagavad Gita 18.78 — Wherever (is) Krishna, the lord of the possessors of mystic power, wherever (is) the (great) archer, the son of Pritha, there in my opinion (are) fortune, victory, prosperity, and eternal justice.
